title: Vladimir Putin, the Humanitarian
excerpt: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian
body: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian

You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again.” — Steve Witkoff, U.S. special envoy to the Middle East, addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin Mark Wednesday, October 21, 2026, as “the day words lost all meaning.” My dictionary just ran outside and threw itself off a bridge
Noah Webster arose from his grave and lurched around, howling and tearing at his hair
Samuel Johnson is bellowing something awful; I can hear it across the Atlantic Ocean
George Orwell is sighing; he has been here before
I have to imagine that Putin is a little insulted at being so gravely misunderstood
With this single word, humanitarian , our envoy has revealed a stunning ignorance of the Russian president’s life’s work

This is like going to Picasso and praising him as a “representational painter,” or calling the Sahara “the wettest place in the world,” or describing Witkoff’s statement as “unembarrassing.” I see, perhaps, where the misunderstanding began

Putin referred to Trump as a “humanitarian,” and Witkoff thought to himself: Ah! This word clearly has a different meaning than I have been led to believe! I will have to reconstruct its definition from context clues
Maybe it’s someone who doesn’t think that the United States should be in NATO
Maybe it’s someone who would look really good on horseback
Maybe no words mean anything! Maybe they are just phonemes to be thrown at a wall, at random, in the manner of that great representational painter Jackson Pollock
One of the conditions of freedom is that words have an understood meaning
If Putin is a humanitarian, then Dolly Parton was an axe murderer

Who else gets to be filed under humanitarian if Putin makes the cut? Stalin? The iceberg that sunk the Titanic? Calling Putin a humanitarian is like calling Hannibal Lecter a humanitarian, although there is more of a case to be made for Hannibal because he does, at least, subsist on people
It is nice and convenient, I think, when words have meaning
When words are more of a suggestion, reality evaporates at your touch, and none of your rights is secure
Good luck getting a sandwich then! Real is fake, fake is real, and all your society’s most precious values carry a disconcerting wink: freedom, free speech, meritocracy, equality
When you chant them, when you promise them to one another, you are not sure exactly what you are saying
Their meaning melts like hot wax, and homeland security becomes an unmarked car slamming into your neighbor

Authoritarians treat words as a game. (Putin, great humanitarian that he is, has some experience with this.) Perhaps war is peace (big news for the Nobel Committee, if true)! Perhaps the best humanitarian is whoever voids the world of the most people! Perhaps election integrity is the exact opposite of that! In the spirit of this new, callous disregard for words and their meaning, I say: Great job! Well done! What a magnificent time to be alive, when all of the best people are in charge.

title: Vivek Ramaswamy’s Appalling Campaign Ad
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture

If you don’t live in Ohio, you’ve probably been blissfully free from thinking about Vivek Ramaswamy since the 2024 Republican presidential primary, which he left after arousing the visceral dislike of pretty much all of his rivals, as well as many voters

Ramaswamy, who’s now running for Ohio governor, is back in the national spotlight this week, once again in extremely unflattering fashion, because of a campaign ad targeting the Democratic candidate Amy Acton

Acton, a first-time candidate, has leaned heavily on her inspiring biography: She has spoken about experiencing homelessness as well as being raped by her stepfather as a child; she later waited tables and delivered newspapers to put herself through medical school, eventually becoming the director of the Ohio Department of Health
Most recent polls have shown Acton with a small advantage over Ramaswamy, which may be why his campaign resorted to the appalling commercial

The spot features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her of being an inveterate liar. “She’s lied her entire life,” Arthur says. “My daughter needs help, and she can’t help you if she needs help herself.” The ad immediately drew both outrage and debunkings. “It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at 12 years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” Acton’s brother said in a statement
National Review , the conservative magazine, pointed out that court documents provide extensive backup for Acton’s claims, as does contemporary press coverage
She was removed from her mother’s custody at the time; her mother’s husband, Cledith Arthur, whom she accused, left the state after being indicted for sexual assault
For a campaign to cast doubt on a rival’s account of childhood sexual abuse is shocking; to do so despite such evidence is despicable
For years, influential MAGA figures insisted that a conspiracy of pedophiles was running the government and other influential institutions
Now some of them treat pedophilia as no big deal

The Trump administration has tried to downplay the case of Jeffrey Epstein, the late sexual predator who was at one time a close friend of the president’s and maintained ties to other administration officials as well
Ramaswamy is opting to dismiss allegations of pedophilia and use them to smear an opponent

At an event earlier this year, he said that Acton has no vision “other than to complain about what someone else did to her.” Despite his previous willingness to mock Acton’s abuse, Ramaswamy’s campaign didn’t initially claim the ad
It first became public on Monday via the colorful Buckeye State political blogger D
The version he posted, received from a tipster, didn’t feature any explanation of who had paid for it

But Ramaswamy has since gone all-in. “It is an ad from our campaign,” Ramaswamy said at an event last night. “I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans

And unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues.” Axios reports that Ramaswamy (who recently loaned his own campaign $5 million) will spend $4 million airing it. “This is a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton,” his campaign manager, Jonathan Ewing, said. “The people who know her best keep warning Ohioans about her.” This is bold, if not wise: The ad has generated widespread condemnation

Even some right-wing influencers who initially spread it, such as Jackie Chea, have had second thoughts : “I have no idea if Amy’s abuse allegations are true, but if they are, then her mother is the monster … I regret framing the post as if Amy was lying about her mother when I can’t be sure about that.” Another, Dan Bostic, wrote , “I’ve never in my life seen someone do something so stupid
It’s hard to even wrap my brain around how someone could possess such horrible political instinct.” (Laura Loomer continues to endorse it , which is telling in its own way
Vice President Vance, meanwhile, was “disgusted”—but by Republican doubters, not by the commercial

He suggested that anything is justified in the name of winning elections. “Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” he said in Cincinnati today, telling his “fellow elected Republicans” to “stop whining about an advertisement.”) On the other side of the aisle, liberals see the ad as suicidal. “I am very confident that this ad will backfire and blow up in Ramaswamy’s face,” Dan Pfeiffer, a former aide to Barack Obama, wrote
Any predictions now are premature: Knowing how convincing the ad will be, compared with the backlash, is impossible
But the ad is another example of how Ramaswamy’s obnoxious personality has turned a race that should have been a safe GOP win into a toss-up
The candidate’s favorability rating is deeply negative
His fellow Republicans continue to dislike him
The outgoing governor, Mike DeWine, whose occasional pangs of conscience make him a profile in near-courage , clearly dreaded endorsing his fellow Republican
And although the national environment is friendly to Democratic candidates this year, no Democrat has won a governor’s race in Ohio since 2006; Donald Trump won the state three times
Acton is a first-time candidate most famous for her association with COVID public-health measures, neither of which is an obvious asset
If Ramaswamy loses, there will be no question about who was responsible

title: Read This Website While You Still Can
excerpt: The internet could be on the verge of a total meltdown
body: The internet could be on the verge of a total meltdown
Yesterday, someone posted to a public forum that two major security flaws had been found in a programming language that undergirds the web
The language, called PHP, is used by as much as 70 percent of websites
In order to protect themselves from hackers, a number of government, hospital, and school websites across Europe went dark this morning
The organization that maintains PHP quickly confirmed it was preparing to announce two major vulnerabilities alongside patches for them
Both weaknesses, officially disclosed today, appear to have existed in PHP for more than a decade but were only just discovered with the use of AI tools
Hackers have already been detected trying to exploit them, likely with the help of AI, and implementing the fixes to address the vulnerabilities could take companies days or weeks

In the meantime, tens of millions of servers, databases, and devices are exposed. “PHP is one of the fundamental pieces of technology that supports the internet,” Sam Rubin, a senior vice president at the cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks, told me

As of now, the websites of the Finnish health agency, the Port of Rotterdam, the Paris police force, 4Chan, and an unknown number of others are all down while they address the PHP vulnerabilities. [ Read: How long until AI hacks everything? ] News of these weaknesses in PHP is the capstone in a weeks-long slew of devastating, AI-powered cybersecurity events

In recent weeks, criminals and state-backed attackers have used AI to hack into more than 100 companies, including John Deere and SharkNinja; to automate hacks on some 400 financial institutions in Latin America; and to steal hundreds of thousands of credit-card records from two companies
Since this summer, attackers have hit governments, data centers, and hospitals in Ukraine, Russia, Argentina, Bangladesh, and Indonesia
Also today, the developers of Node—a platform used by nearly half of software developers—disclosed multiple high-severity vulnerabilities
For the better part of a year, cybersecurity experts have been warning , with mounting alarm , about an impending cyber-apocalypse
For decades, the internet has been riddled with holes and bugs
Code is finicky, and the standard IT approach has been to fix problems when they arise
For decades, the balance held: Skilled hackers are few, and finding and exploiting vulnerabilities takes time
Recent advances in AI have totally upended that equilibrium
Top models have become very good at finding holes and writing malware, and can work much faster than even a team of humans

This is true of both open-source AI systems from China, which can be downloaded and used without restrictions, and the even more capable models from OpenAI and Anthropic, which are continually being jailbroken
The rate of software vulnerabilities identified per month has doubled over the past year
Meanwhile, the time that hackers need to begin exploiting those vulnerabilities—figuring out how to break in and out without being caught—has fallen, by some estimates, from weeks to hours
An actual intrusion, if automated with AI, can take as little as 39 seconds
Historical approaches to detecting and fixing vulnerabilities, or monitoring for suspicious internal activity, are insufficient
AI has created new vulnerabilities, but it also promises to fix them: The vulnerabilities in PHP were discovered independently by a Google-owned cybersecurity company and another effort led by OpenAI
Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic, along with other tech firms, are all working with government agencies around the world to shore up their defenses

But, as numerous cybersecurity experts have told me, there is an asymmetry between attackers and defenders that AI is going to exacerbate: Hackers will use new technology with abandon, while companies are methodical and risk-averse—a hospital or electrical grid can’t risk that an AI security tool unintentionally takes a patient off life support or causes a brownout
And attackers need to find only one hole to succeed, whereas defenders need only one oversight to fail
For a year, criminals and state-backed groups have been experimenting with how to use models to accelerate and automate their attacks
It was only a year ago that Anthropic announced , with great consternation, what it declared to be the first instance of AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage
That still involved a lot of human oversight and required jailbroken Claude agents to work for many hours
Now that the agents are faster and more capable, hackers have gotten more adept at deploying them, and the automation is more extensive

Recent, widespread attacks on South Korean and Japanese websites were reportedly executed by a single Chinese cybercriminal who used AI to target more than 1,000 websites. “This certainly will not be the last large-scale vulnerability identified, because of what’s possible with AI,” Rubin said
The past 24 hours represent a tipping point
Bulking up IT departments, implementing passkeys, and using two-factor authentication remain important
But the most urgent and practical advice being given now is to retreat: Prepare to simply go offline
The NSA advised companies that cannot immediately fix the PHP vulnerability to take down affected digital services
Hospitals, water utilities, and other crucial services are all preparing for hacks by relearning to operate analog
We’re running out of time to prepare for the AI-hacking deluge

title: Why Is Everyone Avoiding the Biggest Issue Facing Voters?
excerpt: Hush! I must hear! It’s an election year, I am a voter, and I need to know the president’s answers to the most pressing questions facing America today: How upho
body: Hush! I must hear! It’s an election year, I am a voter, and I need to know the president’s answers to the most pressing questions facing America today: How upholstered are the chairs in the Rose Garden ? Is the helipad at the White House any good? How are things progressing with the ballroom? And is the golf course going to be ready soon? No, do not ask about affordability
I could not care less about the price of eggs! What am I, a hen? My concerns are more basic

I demand to hear: HOW IS THE HELIPAD? AND IS THAT GOLF COURSE IN EAST POTOMAC PARK BEING DEVELOPED TO THE HIGHEST STANDARDS OF GOLF, TURNING THAT TRASH ISLAND INTO AN ISLAND OF BEAUTY AND SUCCESS? I was up late last night
Pretty high—but that just means the economy is booming
I walked down the hall and looked at my sleeping children

How long could we hope to survive, knowing that at this very moment, in Washington, D.C., a judge is preventing East Potomac Park from becoming one of the world’s great golf courses, instead just letting it lie there, old, tired, beaten up, and useless ? My children say, “Father, Father! When will we be able to afford hamburger?” And I say, “How can you talk about hamburger when you know that Trash Island still needs to be developed to the highest levels and standards of golf?” And they say, “Do you even play golf?” And I say, “ Silence! ” They don’t have their priorities straight
But I’m glad we have a president who does

I hate going to the gas pump, because the numbers there are so high, which I know is a deliberate distraction from the real problems Americans face: the hazardous , dangerous trees on East Potomac Golf Links
After that, I stopped by a restaurant and ate some salad

Immediately, I felt sick to my stomach. “That was tainted lettuce,” my family said. “No,” I said, “it is because of the shame, pertaining to the golf course.” I don’t need a fully staffed FDA monitoring lettuce-borne diseases ! I need to know that we are stopping our assistance to Ukraine in defiance of Congress
I need to know whether Vladimir Putin seemed happy when our president talked to him
I really hope that our president impressed him; Putin is a big, important man
Maybe someday, America will be a world power too
If we can just get this golf course in shape, we can build on that momentum
Don’t you dare say that this isn’t a kitchen-table issue
You haven’t seen my kitchen table, on which a replica of the president’s plans for a truly beautiful arch have sat for the past six months, gathering dust
That arch holds all my dreams. “Why did you buy that and not food?” my children ask
They don’t know what they’re talking about
Don’t try to appeal to me by talking about the cost of living

IRRELEVANT! I want to know: Does the president have a nice-enough plane? Are the right letters on all the buildings in the capital? Good, beautiful letters, such as T , R , U , M , and P —not bad, subpar letters such as K , E , N , N , E , D , Y ? These are my concerns, just as they are the concerns of the whole electorate
For years, I have been unable to hold my head up high, knowing that we don’t have the greatest ballroom slash military complex ever built

How do you think that feels? Every night, I toss and turn, asking myself: Is New Mexico going to keep its disgusting, embarrassing name? Or will it change it to something nice, like New America ? Will they ever manage to cut down those terrifying trees in East Potomac Park, so we can finally feel safe? Hurry, Mr
President! Please, hurry! I don’t know how much longer I can keep living like this.

title: Will the Tech Oligarchs Turn on Trump?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on the growing ca
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on the growing calls for Medicare for All
David discusses how Medicare for All might actually work, why it’s impractical, and why it is fundamentally a promise Democrats cannot keep
Then, David is joined by Kara Swisher to discuss her new podcast with Hillary Clinton, the dangers of unregulated AI, and the power of the AI oligarchs over American politics
David and Kara discuss the potential of an AI bubble and what responsible oversight of AI would look like
Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of The Rise and Fall of American Growth: The U.S
Standard of Living Since the Civil War by Robert Gordon, and whether the AI revolution changes any of Gordon’s pessimistic assessments of what has happened to American growth since 1970
The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Let me ask you about what works and things you’ve changed your mind about
So you have been a career-long advocate for stronger regulation of technology in general— Kara Swisher: David, let me correct you
Frum: What’s your line? “Your local deli is more regulated than the biggest tech platforms in America.” Swisher: Everything. [ Music ] Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum a staff writer at The Atlantic
My guest this week will be Kara Swisher, host of the On With Kara Swisher podcast, and co-host of Pivot , and co-host, very excitingly, of a new podcast that she will co-star [with] Hillary Clinton
And we’ll be talking about that new podcast with Kara
This week’s book is The Rise and Fall of American Growth: The U.S
Standard of Living Since the Civil War by Robert Gordon, an enormously influential book on economic history published a decade ago
And I’ll be discussing whether the advent of the AI revolution changes any of Robert Gordon’s pessimistic assessments of what has happened to American growth since 1970
But before the dialogue with Kara Swisher and before the book discussion, I want to open with some thoughts about the debate over Medicare for All: the slogan, and the idea of Medicare for All
It does look like the next Congress will feature many more advocates of the Medicare for All idea than American politics has seen for a long time
There are bills in Congress purporting to offer or designing or proposing a Medicare for All scheme
Let’s think about this in a real-world way, because we may be talking about this a lot come 2027
What does Medicare for All mean? How would you get there if you were minded to get there? So understand, Medicare, of course, is the program that provides much health insurance for people over 65
It has components with prescription drugs, but the core of it is that it covers medical and hospital bills for people over 65, with some contribution from the over-65s themselves

The Medicare for All proposal is to extend this scheme through all of the American economy, covering everybody through the Medicare program and displacing a lot of the health-care insurance that you have now
Which is mostly—those people who get private health insurance get it usually paid for through an employer, out of the worker’s pay, but through an employer
What would it mean to make this change from a system where much of the health care in the economy is paid for by employer-financed private insurance to one where the U.S
Treasury pays for most health care? So: Half a decade ago, at the end of the 2010s, there was a big study of this
The Congressional Budget Office, and others, too, did a big study of what it would mean to transition to a Medicare for All program
And CBO’s estimate in the year 2020 was that such a program would cost the U.S
Treasury, over the next 10 years, about $30 trillion

But if I think it—if you just figure out prices are higher, you’re going further out into time, you’re starting in 2030 and going to 2040—it’s a good guess that it would cost closer to $40 trillion over 10 years than it would cost to $30 trillion over 10 years
So where would you get the $40 trillion? The U.S
Treasury is going to be spending a lot more
How would it get the extra $40 trillion? Now, proponents of Medicare for All will say—and they’re not completely wrong about this—they will say: Wait a moment
We’re spending the $40 trillion now or thereabouts
That is, you get mostly from your private insurance through your employer
So we’re just taking $40 trillion from this sector of the economy and moving it over to the government, and net-net, it will even out
Maybe it’s a little bit more expensive than what we have now, but not a lot more expensive
Still, we have one way of financing it now, and we’re going to be moved to another way of financing it along the way

How do you make that transition? What would that look like? The proponents of Medicare for All will say this: Look, when you get a job, if you have health care, you are really paying for the health insurance
Your employer lowers your wages to cover the cost and then pays an insurance company, or they self-insure
But in any way, the employer finances the payment of the health coverage out of the wages that you don’t get

title: Like Ken Paxton, Without the Baggage
excerpt: A crucial midterm contest is happening right now in Texas, one that could determine the future of the state and its influence on federal policy and national pol
body: A crucial midterm contest is happening right now in Texas, one that could determine the future of the state and its influence on federal policy and national politics
Senate race—though everyone is watching that one, and with good reason

The Republican, Ken Paxton—who has served as Texas’s attorney general since 2015—is an unusually weak candidate, beset by personal and financial scandals and a reputation for using his office for right-wing culture-war fixations, and weighed down by a deeply unpopular president

On the other side is James Talarico, an unusually strong Democratic candidate, fluent in the language of faith and without the cloud of scandal that haunts his opponent. “This is the most competitive election that we have seen in Texas” in decades, James Henson, the executive director of the University of Texas at Austin’s nonpartisan Texas Politics Project , told me

But the race I’m talking about is downstream of that: Who will succeed Ken Paxton? The two major-party candidates vying to be attorney general are Nathan Johnson, a Democratic state senator from Dallas, and Mayes Middleton (“MAGA Mayes,” as his own ads call him), a Republican state senator and GOP mega-donor whose district covers parts of Harris, Brazoria, and Galveston counties
An October poll from the Texas Politics Project shows a dead heat, with Johnson at 48 percent and Middleton at 47 percent

The Texas attorney general is a very powerful position, one that has frequently been a springboard to higher office—John Cornyn held the job before becoming a U.S. senator, as did Greg Abbott before becoming the state’s governor
The AG is meant to defend the laws of the state, and has certain specific responsibilities, such as enforcing child support and investigating Medicaid fraud

Over the past few decades, however, the role has become something more: a way for ambitious politicians to wage culture wars, cultivate a national profile by taking on right-wing causes, and shape law and policy not just in Texas but nationwide
The attorney general “helps set legal policy across the country,” Justin Nelson, a Democrat who came within a few points of unseating Paxton in 2018, told me
The race between Talarico and Paxton may be capturing everyone’s attention right now, but “when you’re a senator, you’re one of 100,” Nelson pointed out
There’s only one attorney general of Texas

When Abbott was Texas attorney general under the Obama administration, he used to joke , “I go into the office, I sue the federal government and I go home.” Paxton—who was acquitted by the Senate in a 2023 trial over accusations of corruption and bribery—has been even more pugnacious
Early in his tenure as attorney general, Paxton encouraged clerks to refuse to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples

He used the office to sue the developers of a mosque and housing community north of Dallas for securities fraud ; the case fueled right-wing conspiracy theories nationwide about the “Islamization of Texas.” (A state securities commissioner described the case as “horseshit”—ironically, Paxton himself was accused of securities fraud .) He wrote a memo that designated puberty blockers and other gender-affirming health care “child abuse” and that kicked off Child Protective Services investigations of parents of trans children , and most recently used the state’s consumer-protection law to target pediatricians who vaccinate children
He has threatened to investigate public schools to ensure they’re displaying the Ten Commandments
He also filed the case asking the Supreme Court to overturn the results of the 2020 election
He has tried to prevent women whose pregnancies meet the state’s extremely narrow standards for legal abortion from accessing the procedure

After a court order gave one woman whose child had a fatal abnormality permission to get an abortion, Paxton threatened any doctor who dared perform it, warning that the judge’s order “will not insulate hospitals, doctors, or anyone else, from civil and criminal liability.” Paxton has also tried to sue doctors in other states for allegedly providing abortion medication to Texas residents—an issue that is almost certain to end up at the Supreme Court sooner or later, much like Texas’s original abortion bounty law did , in a foreshadowing of the 2022 Dobbs decision overturning Roe v

These cases and others have shaped abortion policy nationally , not just in Texas. [ Read: Ken Paxton is actually doing this ] An entire accounting of Paxton’s use of the AG’s office to further extreme conservative causes would take too long

The Texas AG’s office is the “largest legal power in the conservative movement, nationally, period, end of story,” Adam Piper, who runs the Republican Attorneys General Association, told The Texas Tribune earlier this year

Zaidi, the former director of the Texas House Democratic Caucus, told me that “simply removing a Republican” from the Texas attorney general’s office “could have enormous ripple effects across the country for, frankly, generations to come.” Paxton’s aggressive use of the office isn’t an exclusively right-wing phenomenon; Democratic AGs from California, New York, and other states have been at the forefront of litigation against President Trump’s tariffs, his environmental policies, and his attempt to repeal birthright citizenship
AGs have also pursued consumer-protection issues that the federal government mostly abandoned
But Nathan Johnson is not presenting himself as that kind of candidate

Instead, he says he wants to return the office to what he sees as its traditional role: “It is there to protect consumers from predatory business practices; it is there to investigate shady relationships between the private sector and the public sector; it is there to keep the system of checks and balances in place in government.” This is surely a smart pitch for such a red state, and the race is quite close for a place where Democrats haven’t won statewide office since Pulp Fiction was in theaters

Nevertheless, Texas Republicans’ objections to Paxton are less about policy and more about ethics. “I think Mayes Middleton is a stronger candidate than Ken Paxton,” Nelson said, describing Paxton as perhaps the “most corrupt public official in the country.” Matt Mackowiak, a Republican political consultant, told me that Middleton’s policy views “align with a majority of Texans.” This state has been red for three decades
Voters may be tired of Paxton’s baggage, but that doesn’t mean they’re tired of having a state attorney general who tries to move the state and the country in a conservative direction

W hoever becomes the next attorney general, he’ll be tasked with enforcing Texas law, which includes that near ban on abortion and a series of restrictions on trans rights that frightened some families so much that they ultimately fled the state

But there’s a difference between enforcing the law and what Paxton has done, which is interpret the law so aggressively that, for example, a pregnant woman whose fetus has a fatal abnormality has to leave the state just to get care

Johnson told me that Paxton’s attempt to sue doctors in New York, Delaware, and California over abortion medication that is banned in Texas was “legally ridiculous.” Texas law, he said, does not apply outside of Texas
Johnson said he is “not opposed to immigration enforcement” but that he would sue the federal government if immigration authorities violate Texas residents’ constitutional rights

He called the law passed last year requiring public schools to display the Ten Commandments unconstitutional, and said he would not strong-arm any schools who declined to follow the law “until the Supreme Court says otherwise.” He also decried Paxton’s effort to use driver’s-license data from the Department of Public Safety to create a registry of transgender Texans

Johnson’s approach, he suggested, would be to simply leave trans people alone. “We’re talking about not abusing your power to make certain people miserable, to rally your base,” he said. “And I’m happy to say that I don’t think that kind of behavior is being rewarded politically right now in Texas.” [ Carlos Sanchez: How Texas’s attorney general won by losing big ] Still, Texas has arguably gotten redder in the past six years
Trump beat Hillary Clinton in the state in 2016 by nine points, Biden by about six, and Harris by about 14
Even in a midterm year with an unpopular incumbent president weighing down the GOP ticket, Democrats have a lot to overcome

In the candidates’ most recent campaign-finance reports, Johnson had taken in a little more than $1 million, whereas Middleton—the inheritor of his father’s oil-and-gas company—had almost $3.5 million in contributions
That money could make a big difference, especially since neither candidate has much name recognition
In the Texas Politics Project poll, 40 percent of voters had no opinion of Middleton, and 48 percent had no opinion of Johnson
But Zaidi told me that Johnson, being part of the class-of-2018 Democrats who entered office during Trump’s first term, was well equipped to compete in Texas

These officials know how to take on big “policy fights, but in a way that’s not a turnoff for the median voter,” Zaidi said, pointing to Johnson’s work trying to expand Medicaid in Texas —a popular policy but one that Republican state lawmakers have blocked

title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Introducing: the Impossible issue We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas
Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains
But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful
That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue
We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood , build cities on the moon , and attain cognitive immortality
We investigate AI’s ability to say no , a bionic eye that can restore sight , and high hopes for blended meat
Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years
This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no
Subscribe now to read the full print issue
Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon Large language models are set to go lunar
A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month
The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment
But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation

Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration . —Tereza Pultarova How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost
It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time
The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects
As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss
Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead

Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster . —James Temple MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought
MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up
He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts
Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Elon Musk reportedly ordered the recent Starlink slowdown in Ukraine The restrictions hampered drone strikes and air defences. ( WSJ $) + The move sparked confusion in Washington over who authorised it. ( CNBC ) + Ukraine’s volunteer army is keeping Starlink alive. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 An OpenAI model disabled its own safety checks—then lied about it Two agents weakened the company’s safeguards during routine tasks. ( CNBC ) + They turned off systems designed to spot their misbehaviour. ( FT $) + Here’s why AI agents lie to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 SpaceX and Tesla have begun merger discussions They’ve formed special committees to discuss a deal. ( BBC ) + Elon Musk, the CEO of both companies, said it’s “a good idea.” ( Axios ) + A merger could combine their AI and manufacturing plans. ( Reuters $) 4 Global emissions have stalled, but warming is heading towards 2.8°C The UN says the 1.5°C climate target is now out of reach. ( Nature ) + Current pledges would still bring warming to 2.1°C. ( New Scientist $) + Climate tech companies offer rays of hope. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Ukraine says it’s carried out the world’s first drone evacuation A heavy hexacopter flew a soldier to safety. ( Ars Technica ) + Ukraine has shared a video showing the evacuation. ( CNBC ) + A Russian satellite recently stalked a spacecraft believed to support Ukraine. ( NYT $) 6 Meta has paused Muse sharing after private chats surfaced online Researchers found 6,800 links exposing sensitive conversations. ( Verge ) + AI agents are not your “coworkers.” ( MIT Technology Review ) 7 More than 1,000 mathematicians have pledged to shun AI companies Some also vowed to avoid AI tools in their research. ( New Scientist $) 8 AI is making it easy to clone almost any software Viral tools promise easy copying, but often produce slop. ( 404 Media ) 9 A computer program has finally outdone humans at cryptic crosswords Its creator hopes to tackle the harder challenge of setting puzzles. ( Guardian ) 10 A newly-discovered particle could explain the origins of reality In particular, it could reveal why matter survived the Big Bang. ( 404 Media ) Quote of the day “I did not remove an enabled monitor from it.”  —GPT-6 Astra, an OpenAI coding agent, tells its user it hasn’t disabled a safeguard after doing exactly that, the company reveals in a new misalignment report
One more thing This giant microwave may change the future of war US armed forces are hunting for a weapon that disables drones en masse—and they want it fast

One solution focuses on microwaves: high-powered electronic devices that push out kilowatts of power to zap the circuits of a drone as if it were the tinfoil you forgot to take off your leftovers when you heated them up
Defense tech startup Epirus may have the winning formula
The company has developed a cutting-edge, cost-efficient drone zapper that’s sparking the interest of the US military—and drones are just one of its targets

Peer into its crosshairs . —Sam Dean We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Don’t feel guilty about enjoying a siesta; fish take naps during the day, too. + Every trade has its go-to tools

This site has built a fascinating register of them . + Wikipop spotlights what was most popular on Wikipedia yesterday, providing a daily snapshot of what the world is reading. + Meet the self-taught woodcarver who went from a broke young father to creating some of Disneyland’s most iconic attractions .

title: We can do impossible things
excerpt: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve got
body: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”  I won’t lie
It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag
I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head
I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items

Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.) My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality
Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here
This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine
If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize
We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well)

But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now.  We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment
To be a little … audacious.  Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas
It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing
That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular.  We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas
Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains
Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems

But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with.  It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful

And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken

Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible.  Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem
They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature

But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.  So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no

title: Nuclear-powered spaceships
excerpt: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom
body: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom
SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029

A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales
The sticking points Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not
The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites

And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.” Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going
The US has started—and terminated— several programs looking into it over the past 75 years
The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which ended in 2025

The project was canceled because of high experimentation costs, an inability to compete with conventional rocket propulsion on price, and difficulty ensuring that ground tests could be performed safely and effectively. (You are creating an incredibly powerful nuclear reaction, after all.) The progress After much wavering, it now appears that nuclear-powered interplanetary travel is a $2 billion bet NASA is willing to make

The agency is pursuing an approach called nuclear electric propulsion, which uses the neutrons produced in a self-­sustaining, uranium-­atom-splitting reaction to create heat and ultimately electricity
The electricity is used to ionize a gas, which is blasted out of the spacecraft with the help of magnetic fields, generating thrust

The approach “is very low thrust, but very efficient,” says Sebastian Corbisiero, the US Department of Energy’s national technical director of space reactor programs. “So you can use it for a long period of time.” What might such a rocket look like? A presentation by Steve Sinacore, program director of NASA’s SR-1 program, offers some clues
So far, the concept art makes the craft look like a colossal fletched arrow

The back will house the power-and-propulsion system, while the tip will hold a uranium-filled nuclear reactor with a capacity of at least 20 kilowatts. (For context, a typical nuclear plant on Earth is about 50,000 times more powerful.) The “fletches” on SR-1 are large fins that help cool the reactor by radiating heat into space

Like many other pieces of space hardware, the reactor will need to be put through its paces on the ground before it’s cleared for the rough rocket trip to space. “Going through the launch safely is going to be a challenge,” says Middleburgh. “You are being shaken, rattled, and rolled.” For safety reasons, the reactor will be switched on around two days post-launch, when it’s comfortably far from Earth
Uranium isn’t tremendously dangerous by itself, but that can’t be said of the waste products that emerge when the reactor is running
If SR-1 works as planned, its journey to Mars will take about a year.  Will this novel form of space propulsion actually reach the Red Planet by 2029? It’s possible

NASA says the Idaho National Laboratory, which is building SR-1’s reactor, is making progress and is on target for a late-2028 launch. “Procurement of major components is underway, and integration work on the power and propulsion element is advancing steadily,” Sinacore told MIT Technology Review

The outlook will get even sunnier if the Artemis program, which aims to start laying the foundations for a base on the lunar south pole by the decade’s end, keeps to its own bold deadline.  “It’s an aggressive timeline,” says Lindsey Holmes, who is vice president of advanced projects at Analytical Mechanics Associates, an aerospace company in Virginia
She suspects the push is being driven partly by China’s and Russia’s own deep-space nuclear ambitions
The two countries have spoken about plans to place a reactor on the moon’s surface in the mid-2030s to power a jointly operated lunar base

Whether it flies or fails in space, SR-1’s development should help NASA put its own reactor on the moon; the technology involved in the two projects is broadly similar, given that the lunar surface, like space itself, is a vacuum
If an interplanetary nuclear-powered spacecraft works, a nuclear reactor on the moon should too
Progress meter . . . . . . . . . . . . 6 Most of the technology for SR-1 already exists; it’s going to come down to piecing it all together and then seeing how it performs in space.

title: Exercise in a pill
excerpt: It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood
body: It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood
By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout

The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.  The sticking points It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health
But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step
Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs
That’s a tall order: More than 90% of treatments that enter human studies fail

The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia
The progress There may never be a pill that delivers all the benefits of exercise, but research could lead to new medicines that mimic some aspects of working out

Scientists have already identified many important exercise-related signals and have even developed compounds to regulate them. (Some preliminary results have been so promising that doping authorities have proactively banned the compounds.)  Burris and his colleagues are focused on a receptor that’s always switched on, even without exercise
Working out appears to boost that receptor in muscle cells, which in turn helps bolster endurance over time
Burris’s lab has spent years designing a drug that cranks up the receptor’s activity directly, and mice treated with the drug ran longer and farther than mice that weren’t
They “become marathon mice without having to do any type of exercise,” Burris says
There are even indications—also in mice—that the compound mimics some of the cognitive benefits of exercise and could help treat heart failure
Burris founded a company called Pelagos to carry the work forward into a clinical trial
Other workout-mimicking drugs have already entered human studies
In June, the biotech firm Cambrian Bio reported that its experimental drug ATX-304 boosted metabolism and reduced liver and belly fat in people with obesity and prediabetes

It activates a metabolic switch that helps cells sense when energy supplies dip and coordinates the production of more fuel—the same switch that helps us sustain long sessions jumping rope or swimming laps

Cambrian hopes it will help people lose weight without losing muscle, a common concern with GLP-1 medicines.   Progress meter ………… 5 Our understanding of how exercise benefits the body is still coming into focus, and drug development is prone to failure.

title: Interspecies communication
excerpt: Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us
body: Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us

Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech
The sticking points Teasing all this out is complex
To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them
Prairie dogs, for example, utter a different series of yips when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby
It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-­observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats
Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive

And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate.  The progress Over the past 50 years, a growing arsenal of devices has made it easier to observe the sophisticated ways animals communicate

Hydrophones at the bottom of the ocean can capture humpback whale song, and tiny wearable “ biologgers ” can record a bat’s every squeak.  In the last decade, advances in AI have leveled up our ability to make sense of it all
The technology can detect different calls, distinguish which sounds belong to which animal, and spot patterns

Researchers at the Earth Species Project (ESP), a nonprofit founded in 2018 to decode animal communication, recently used machine learning to detect vocalizations of carrion crows and determine which bird made which call.  They suspect that more advanced AI could translate critters’ chatter
Large language models like Claude and ChatGPT excel at finding relationships between words, explains Sara Keen, one of ESP’s behavioral ecologists
ESP hopes its own NatureLM—trained on human speech, music, and animal sounds—will be able to interpret the vocalizations of a variety of species.  That promise, however, is still theoretical

Yossi Yovel, a neuroecologist at Tel Aviv University, worries that these models will put too much emphasis on acoustic similarities and make mistakes—like lumping together similar sounds that have different meanings.  As for a two-way convo? It’s not clear when—or whether—that will happen

Still, “a lot of animals have an evolutionary structure that is similar enough that we should be able to understand what they’re saying,” Slobodchikoff says.  Progress meter ………… 4 Researchers have amassed heaps of data on animal communication, but they’re still trying to figure out how to decipher it all.

title: Cleaning up PFAS
excerpt: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a
body: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a
PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet
Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays , cancer , and reduced immune response

They are known for a strong bond between carbon and fluorine, which the environment struggles to break down.  The sticking points PFAS are everywhere: They spew from factories and slough off products and into water with normal use
Scientists have found them in everything from human blood to Antarctic snow

One 2022 report found that 89% of the US population had PFAS in excess of two nanograms per milliliter of blood plasma, a common threshold for potential adverse health effects, and 9% of the population had passed the riskier level of 20 nanograms per milliliter
New compounds are still being created and used

There are more than 12,000 of them, and much of the cleanup research focuses on only a small handful.  The progress Cleansing PFAS-contaminated soil is a project in its infancy, but it is possible to prevent more buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems
There are two ways to handle this: trap or destroy

Some scientists have found reverse osmosis—a process that pushes water through supertight filters—useful in point-of-use cases, like water filters at kitchen sinks .  Other techniques in the pipeline might be more suitable for large-scale removal—for example, at water treatment facilities
One, called foam fractionation , generates bubbles that capture PFAS
More approaches, like ensnaring the chemicals in nanothin layers of charged metal, are also under investigation.  Trapping, though, is imperfect

You’re left with PFAS-filled brine, which if not properly destroyed (an expensive and energy-sucking endeavor) can still end up in the environment.  Jack Huang, a professor of crop and soil sciences at the University of Georgia, is working on destruction
He’s testing a method called electrochemical degradation , which uses electrodes to break down the bonds that hold PFAS together
The product destroyed more than 90% of PFAS mass in tests and has already been licensed by the engineering consulting firm AECOM .  Ridding life of PFAS is also a policy challenge
There are alternatives; we just need the push to use them
And we’ve had success before: The EPA’s 2010/2015 PFOA Stewardship Program has helped slash the release of water-repellent perfluorooctanoic acid by 95%

More recently, Minnesota, Maine, and New Mexico have passed bans on PFAS in products like cookware and dental floss.  Progress meter ………… 6 Scientists are making strides toward removing and destroying PFAS—but it’ll be all for naught if we don’t turn off the tap.

title: Chiricahua is the nation’s newest national park – what does that mean?
url:
<title>Chiricahua is the nation’s newest national park – what does that mean?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766817/original/file-20261016-50-ymrfah.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C85%2C2048%2C1365&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A large rock balanced atop another is one of the striking features of the Chiricahua landscape.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chiricahua_balanced_rock.jpg">Pretzelpaws via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>With a stroke of a pen, President Donald Trump has officially created the United States’ <a href="https://www.nps.gov/chir/learn/news/chiricahua-national-monument-becomes-america-s-newest-national-park.htm">64th national park</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nps.gov/chir/index.htm">Chiricahua</a>, in southeastern Arizona, was established as a <a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/faraway-ranch-chiricahua-national-monument.htm">national monument in April 1924</a> to protect its towering rhyolite hoodoos – tall spires of rock – and diversity of wildlife. The mountainous landscape is commonly known as a “wonderland of rocks.”</p>

<p>An <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/6380">act of Congress</a>, signed by Trump, has now designated the 12,000-acre property a national park, the flagship label of the National Park Service system. It joins the <a href="https://www.nps.gov/grca/index.htm">Grand Canyon</a>, <a href="https://www.nps.gov/pefo/index.htm">Petrified Forest</a> and <a href="https://www.nps.gov/sagu/index.htm">Saguaro</a> as the fourth national park in Arizona.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://sites.google.com/view/sethkannarr/">geographer</a> who studies parks and the naming of places, I have seen that when a National Park Service property is redesignated as a national park, the new label doesn’t typically include much change for the site itself beyond signs and branding.</p>

<p>There’s not usually more money available to manage or protect the site. But the new title serves political purposes and could mean quite a lot to visitors, supporters and surrounding communities alike in the coming years.</p>

<h2>How parks are designated</h2>

<p>The National Park Service <a href="https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/national-park-system.htm">manages 433 properties, which it calls units</a>, with <a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/nps-designations.htm">19 different designations</a>, such as “national battlefields,” “national lakeshores” and “national scenic trails.” Only <a href="https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/national-park-system.htm">64 of these units</a> carry the formal title or designation of “national park.”</p>

<p>All but one of these categories can be bestowed only by Congress. National monuments can be created by the president directly, under the provisions of the <a href="https://theconversation.com/national-monuments-have-grown-and-shrunk-under-us-presidents-for-over-a-century-thanks-to-one-law-the-antiquities-act-252707">Antiquities Act of 1906</a>.</p>

<p>For example, the Antiquities Act has been at the center of a decade-long controversy over the size of <a href="https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/12/28/proclamation-establishment-bears-ears-national-monument">Bears Ears National Monument</a>, which President Barack Obama created to protect 1.3 million acres in Utah in December 2016. That same act allowed Trump to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2021/apr/08/deb-haaland-bears-ears-national-monument">shrink the protected area to 200,000 acres</a> in 2017 and President Joe Biden to <a href="https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/10/08/a-proclamation-on-bears-ears-national-monument/">reexpand it to 1.3 million acres</a> in 2021. In 2026, <a href="https://www.sltrib.com/news/environment/2026/07/15/here-are-new-maps-bears-ears-grand/">Trump slashed it again, to 121,000 acres</a>.</p>

<h2>Why redesignations make a difference</h2>

<p>My previous analysis of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-74653-6_8">contentious redesignation</a> of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial in St. Louis to <a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/index.htm">Gateway Arch National Park</a> in 2018 found that it was not done to offer additional protection for this monument to the United States’ Western exploration and growth.</p>

<p>Rather, the move was meant to take advantage of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.32469/10355/91514">public significance of the “national park” label</a> and thereby attract more tourists and tourism revenue to the local economy.</p>

<p>The effort to make it a national park was part of a <a href="https://www.archpark.org/updates/news/gateway-arch-national-park-designated-new-name-for-park">local campaign to renovate the underground visitor center</a>, revitalize the park grounds and increase tourism. But the <a href="https://www.congress.gov/115/plaws/publ128/PLAW-115publ128.pdf">law that formalized the change</a> included no additional funding, resources or protections for the Gateway Arch.</p>

<p>Changing the designation contradicted the park service’s own declaration that the term “national park” should be used for an area that “<a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/nps-designations.htm">contains a variety of resources</a> and encompasses large land or water areas to help provide adequate protection of the resources.” </p>

<p>During congressional hearings, the deputy director of the National Park Service, Robert Vogel, recommended the Gateway Arch not be labeled a national park but rather a national monument, because it “<a href="https://www.doi.gov/ocl/s-1438">is too small and limited</a> in the range of resources the site protects and interprets to be called a national park.”</p>

<p>Gateway Arch National Park is now the smallest-area park in the U.S., at less than 200 acres, and is home to a <a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/planyourvisit/the-significance-of-the-gateway-arch-landscape.htm">large steel arch, an open lawn area, a museum and a single historic building</a> – a courthouse where <a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/planyourvisit/och.htm">one of the Dred Scott trials</a> was heard, along with other civil rights cases.</p>

<p>However, it does not provide opportunities to view wildlife in its natural habitat, spectacular geologic features, diverse outdoor recreation opportunities or a sense of wilderness that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-74653-6_8">the public has come to expect from national parks</a>.</p>

<p>The park’s website admits “<a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/learn/nature/plants.htm">it is unusual for a national park to have no natural plant life</a>” and describes the park as adjacent to the “<a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/learn/nature/animals.htm">concrete jungle of downtown St. Louis</a>.”</p>

<p>Although Chiricahua’s <a href="https://www.wbaltv.com/article/chiricahua-national-monument-new-national-park-arizona/74065478">rocky landscapes</a> and archaeological evidence of <a href="https://chiricahuaapachenation.org/">long-standing Indigenous use and occupation</a> more closely resembles what <a href="https://doi.org/10.32469/10355/91514">many people expect for a national park</a>, it likely will receive some of the same <a href="https://www.outsideonline.com/adventure-travel/national-parks/gateway-arch-national-park-46/">public critique</a> that the Gateway Arch and other national parks redesignated during the first Trump administration have received.</p>

<h2>Potential ‘new’ national parks on the horizon</h2>

<p>In rare cases, a community, group or other organization proposes adding an area that is not currently managed by the National Park Service to the system, but that process <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RS20158">takes a lot of time</a>.</p>

<p>It is more common to change the formal designation of a property already within the system, as has happened with this redesignation of Chiricahua.</p>

<p>Similarly, Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore became <a href="https://www.nps.gov/indu/index.htm">Indiana Dunes National Park</a> in 2019. That same year, White Sands National Monument in New Mexico became <a href="https://www.nps.gov/whsa/index.htm">White Sands National Park</a>. And in 2020, New River Gorge National River in West Virginia became <a href="https://www.nps.gov/neri/index.htm">New River Gorge National Park and Preserve</a>.</p>

<p>There are redesignation efforts underway seeking to make national parks in other locations as well, including the <a href="https://www.backpacker.com/news-and-events/news/delaware-water-gap-national-park/">Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area</a> in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, <a href="https://tiffany.house.gov/media/press-releases/rep-tiffany-reintroduces-bill-create-wisconsins-first-national-park">Apostle Islands National Lakeshore</a> in Wisconsin, and <a href="https://norton.house.gov/media/press-releases/norton-introduces-bill-rename-rock-creek-park-rock-creek-national-park-0">Rock Creek Park</a> in the District of Columbia.</p>

<p>In my measure, it is simply a waiting game to see whether these National Park Service sites will also be redesignated to national parks.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What will actually change for Chiricahua?</h2>

<p>Making Chiricahua a national park was a bipartisan effort – co-sponsored by Arizona U.S. Reps. Juan Ciscomani, a Republican, and Greg Stanton, a Democrat – that has received some opposition for several reasons.</p>

<p>The complaints have highlighted <a href="https://www.rvtravel.com/if-chiricahua-becomes-a-national-park-expect-crowds-why-that-matters//">fears that the new label will bring increased tourism</a> and overcrowding in what is considered a <a href="https://nationalparkobsessed.com/chiricahua-be-a-national-park/">small park with limited infrastructure</a>. Now that Chiricahua has been redesignated, the potential influx of new visitors in the coming years could affect the more <a href="https://www.rvtravel.com/if-chiricahua-becomes-a-national-park-expect-crowds-why-that-matters/">personal and isolated experience</a> that they currently appreciate.</p>

<p>However, the only real changes in these places would be in marketing – the signs, <a href="https://www.nps.gov/subjects/hfc/a-brief-history-of-the-unigrid.htm">brochures</a> and merchandise sold in gift shops. But these changes have an important effect: The tagline of “new national park” <a href="https://headwaterseconomics.org/public-lands/protected-lands/national-monuments-redesignated-national-parks/">markets well</a> to <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R41816">potential visitors</a>.</p>

<p>But the funding that Chiricahua receives from the federal government will not change, and the label of “national park” won’t actually protect this landscape any better than it already is under the stewardship of the National Park Service.</p>
