<title>An AI model’s false tip to Philadelphia police reveals how digital agents can do as they’re told and still cause trouble</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766819/original/file-20261016-50-jx2dj3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2506%2C1670&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">An AI agent was instructed to invent and carry out sample tasks on randomly chosen webpages. It went to a Philadelphia Police Department website and submitted a made-up tip about an unsolved homicide.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Deadly%20Police%20Pursuits/eadbb69554fc463493d99f1943acc3b4/photo">AP Photo/Matt Rourke</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>An anonymous tip arrived on PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a website run by the Philadelphia Police Department, on July 18, 2026.</p>

<p>“I may have information regarding this case,” it stated, and claimed the writer had seen someone matching the suspect’s description near the scene of a crime.</p>

<p>The tip was false. The page described no suspect, and the informer was, in fact, Claude Haiku 4.5, an AI model made by San Francisco-based Anthropic. </p>

<p>The tip was flagged as spam and never reached detectives. Anthropic found it in late September while reviewing its own test records. They alerted police on Oct. 8 and described the incident in <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions">a report</a> they published Oct. 9. <a href="https://6abc.com/post/anthropic-ai-model-submitted-false-tip-unsolved-murder-philadelphia-police-say/19925243/">Philadelphia police disclosed it</a> that day as well.</p>

<h2>An uncontrolled test</h2>

<p>AI companies now build “<a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-an-ai-agent-a-computer-scientist-explains-the-next-wave-of-artificial-intelligence-tools-242586">agents</a>,” versions of their chatbots that can operate a web browser, click buttons and fill in forms on a user’s behalf. To measure how well an agent does this, companies run it through thousands of practice tasks, often live on the internet.</p>

<p>According to Anthropic, the false tip was generated during a routine test of the model. </p>

<p>In this test, Haiku 4.5 was told to invent sample tasks on randomly chosen webpages and then carry them out. One of those pages happened to be about an unsolved Philadelphia homicide, and it had a tip form.</p>

<p>The model’s instructions listed things it must never do: Log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases and submit anything destructive. </p>

<p>Submit a form was not on the list. </p>

<p>So, the model wrote a plausible-sounding tip, left the optional name and contact boxes blank, and clicked submit. </p>

<p>Anthropic says the test records indicate the tip was generated as sample content for a practice task, not to mislead police.</p>

<p>The police tip was one of several incidents in Anthropic’s report. In another incident, a research model was supposed to practice on a copy of a government form. When the copy failed to load, it went to the real government website and submitted the form there. Other Claude models found <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/anthropic-cant-reliably-control-its-ai-agents-its-cutting-off-its-internal-evals-from-the-live-internet-instead/">ways around paywalls and access limits</a> to reach data they needed.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Man wearing tie and classes appears on video monitors in front of people seated at long table" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766820/original/file-20261016-60-8wjssg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766820/original/file-20261016-60-8wjssg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766820/original/file-20261016-60-8wjssg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766820/original/file-20261016-60-8wjssg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766820/original/file-20261016-60-8wjssg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766820/original/file-20261016-60-8wjssg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766820/original/file-20261016-60-8wjssg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, speaks remotely during a U.N. Security Council meeting on artificial intelligence on Sept. 23, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/UN%20General%20Assembly%20AI/9a6f62e8832442a6b135f38820880a96/photo">AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Why would an AI do this</h2>

<p>Anthropic attributes these incidents to the persistence of its software. When the model can’t finish a task the way it was told, it finds a work-around instead of stopping to ask the human who gave it its initial task. </p>

<p>That habit comes partly from how these systems learn – much of their skill is built through trial and error. The model attempts a task many times and is rewarded when it succeeds. If the training accidentally rewards cutting corners, the model learns that cutting corners pays. Researchers call this “<a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/emergent-misalignment-reward-hacking">reward hacking</a>.” A human student drilled only on getting the right answer, by any means necessary, might learn the same lesson.</p>

<p>However, instructions given to an AI agent are never complete. A human worker who is told “Don’t buy anything or log in” would still know not to send police a made-up eyewitness account. But the model has no such common sense to fall back on. It treated a list of forbidden actions as the full boundary of acceptable behavior.</p>

<p>This is also why these models “<a href="https://theconversation.com/what-are-ai-hallucinations-why-ais-sometimes-make-things-up-242896">hallucinate</a>,” making things up. AI agents are built to produce fluent, plausible text. Asked to fill a tip form with an example, the model wrote what a tip typically sounds like, with no regard for the truthfulness of its content.</p>

<h2>Should we be worried?</h2>

<p>As a <a href="https://drexel.edu/law/faculty/fulltime_fac/Anat%20Lior/">law professor</a> who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=GpaqMhAAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">studies AI governance</a>, two concerns stand out for me: scale and control.</p>

<p>The larger concern is scale. AI agents are moving out of the lab and into products people already use. Google’s Chrome browser now has a feature called <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/16821166?hl=en">auto browse</a> that lets its Gemini assistant click through websites and fill in forms. Perplexity’s <a href="https://www.perplexity.ai/comet">Comet browser</a> and Anthropic’s <a href="https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12012173-get-started-with-claude-in-chrome">Claude in Chrome extension</a> do the same.</p>

<p>Every task a person hands to an agent is another chance for something to go wrong. If agents carry out a million tasks a day, a mistake that happens only once in 10,000 tasks would happen about 100 times a day. Those mistakes could mean false reports that take up police time, benefits or loan applications filed with wrong information, or payments and bookings the user never approved.</p>

<p>Anthropic itself notes that <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions">several incidents happened</a> during ordinary use of Claude Haiku 4.5, not just testing. OpenAI has similarly reported its own agents <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/ai-agents-false-homicide-tip-anthropic-claude-9.7377169">reaching government sites in unplanned ways</a>.</p>

<p>AI companies can’t fully control their agents, and that may lead to more harm and to gaps in who is held liable. These types of harms could include <a href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/legal-exchange-insights-and-commentary/courts-navigating-ai-defamation-opens-legal-risks-for-companies">defamation</a>, <a href="https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-definitions/what-is-bias-in-ai">bias</a>, <a href="https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/generative-ai-social-engineering">deceit and social engineering</a> and <a href="https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/these-are-most-urgent-ai-risks-according-to-272-experts">much more</a>. It might seem fair not to hold a company responsible for actions it couldn’t control. But in cases like these, no other person or organization clearly controls the agent either, which could leave people who were harmed by the AI agent without anyone to hold legally responsible.</p>

<p>In my view, AI agents should be told what they may do, not just what they may not do, and anything AI companies send into the real world should be checked first. Until those safeguards are standard, any public online form, from a police tip line to a benefits application, could be receiving AI-written submissions that lack intuition and common sense. Their errors could, for example, <a href="https://www.preventionweb.net/news/ai-generated-misinformation-can-create-confusion-and-hinder-responses-during-emergencies">deprive resources from real emergencies</a> or <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2024/11/20/ai-benefit-programs-doge-techtonic-justice/">deny benefits a person is entitled to</a>. Meanwhile, victims of that harm may struggle to get compensation due to the lack of clarity around who had control over the AI agent. </p>

body: An AI agent was instructed to invent and carry out sample tasks on randomly chosen webpages
It went to a Philadelphia Police Department website and submitted a made-up tip about an unsolved homicide

AP Photo/Matt Rourke An anonymous tip arrived on PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a website run by the Philadelphia Police Department, on July 18, 2026. “I may have information regarding this case,” it stated, and claimed the writer had seen someone matching the suspect’s description near the scene of a crime
The page described no suspect, and the informer was, in fact, Claude Haiku 4.5, an AI model made by San Francisco-based Anthropic
The tip was flagged as spam and never reached detectives
Anthropic found it in late September while reviewing its own test records
They alerted police on Oct. 8 and described the incident in a report they published Oct. 9
Philadelphia police disclosed it that day as well
An uncontrolled test AI companies now build “ agents ,” versions of their chatbots that can operate a web browser, click buttons and fill in forms on a user’s behalf
To measure how well an agent does this, companies run it through thousands of practice tasks, often live on the internet
According to Anthropic, the false tip was generated during a routine test of the model
In this test, Haiku 4.5 was told to invent sample tasks on randomly chosen webpages and then carry them out
One of those pages happened to be about an unsolved Philadelphia homicide, and it had a tip form
The model’s instructions listed things it must never do: Log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases and submit anything destructive
So, the model wrote a plausible-sounding tip, left the optional name and contact boxes blank, and clicked submit
Anthropic says the test records indicate the tip was generated as sample content for a practice task, not to mislead police
The police tip was one of several incidents in Anthropic’s report
In another incident, a research model was supposed to practice on a copy of a government form
When the copy failed to load, it went to the real government website and submitted the form there
Other Claude models found ways around paywalls and access limits to reach data they needed
Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, speaks remotely during a U.N
Security Council meeting on artificial intelligence on Sept. 23, 2026
AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura Why would an AI do this Anthropic attributes these incidents to the persistence of its software
When the model can’t finish a task the way it was told, it finds a work-around instead of stopping to ask the human who gave it its initial task
That habit comes partly from how these systems learn – much of their skill is built through trial and error
The model attempts a task many times and is rewarded when it succeeds
If the training accidentally rewards cutting corners, the model learns that cutting corners pays
Researchers call this “ reward hacking .” A human student drilled only on getting the right answer, by any means necessary, might learn the same lesson
However, instructions given to an AI agent are never complete
A human worker who is told “Don’t buy anything or log in” would still know not to send police a made-up eyewitness account
But the model has no such common sense to fall back on
It treated a list of forbidden actions as the full boundary of acceptable behavior
This is also why these models “ hallucinate ,” making things up
AI agents are built to produce fluent, plausible text
Asked to fill a tip form with an example, the model wrote what a tip typically sounds like, with no regard for the truthfulness of its content
Should we be worried? As a law professor who studies AI governance , two concerns stand out for me: scale and control
AI agents are moving out of the lab and into products people already use
Google’s Chrome browser now has a feature called auto browse that lets its Gemini assistant click through websites and fill in forms
Perplexity’s Comet browser and Anthropic’s Claude in Chrome extension do the same
Every task a person hands to an agent is another chance for something to go wrong

<title>Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767027/original/file-20261019-50-xu5oi9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6427%2C4284&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">President Donald Trump&#39;s offer to pay out $5,000 checks if Republicans win belongs to a long political tradition of cash for votes.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Trump/e68092bb4c9a4a6587141c60cef1f782/photo">AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win. </p>

<p>President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/20/business/dealbook/trump-doge-dividend.html">DOGE dividend</a>” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/17/us/politics/trump-cash-payments.html">rebates from tariff revenues</a>, and a diversion of money currently used to <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-90-medicare-rebate-rolls-out-but-millions-arent-eligible-critics-see-a-political-stunt">subsidize health insurance companies</a> directly to Americans. </p>

<p>But his pledge to give <a href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-dividend-5k-5000-check-republicans-cc80644e3168acd31c892129fb849436">US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen</a> if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-anti-bribery-laws-apply-to-trumps-promise-of-5-000-payments-if-republicans-keep-control-of-congress-291722">raises concerns from a legal point of view</a>.</p>

<p>For this to actually happen, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/5-000-checks-for-every-american-what-to-know-about-trumps-latest-promise-0eb47fe6">it needs congressional approval</a> – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/congressional-vote-2026.html">margins are tight in key races</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.kenneth-greene.com/">I’m a political scientist</a> who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote. </p>

<h2>Why vote buying rarely works</h2>

<p>The practice dates back to <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/203895">ancient Rome</a> and was a staple of <a href="https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/8176/bosses-machines-and-urban-voters?srsltid=AU7gw4VGJg4ujCoq-ruuKiW-fWMmPShERfwKPvMxwmxBT-RHKKEiZzrb">American political machines</a> from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia. </p>

<p>By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/rainbows-end/paper">newly arrived immigrants</a>. Institutional reforms, including the <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691000442/political-parties-and-the-state?srsltid=AU7gw4Xsq6o_EBfxqUKm05PlMcr70bk38TRiWatgCiPNKxuy_-X7ggWD">professionalization of government bureaucracies</a> at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s. </p>

<p>But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009776738">73 countries</a> offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes. </p>

<p>If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/against-the-machine/57F1F293192A9A88E8A4731185D3A425">vote-buying attempts</a> across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence.</p>

<p>Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26379534">truly indifferent</a>.</p>

<p>As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “<a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/against-the-machine/57F1F293192A9A88E8A4731185D3A425">Against the Machine</a>.” </p>

<h2>The importance of competition</h2>

<p>There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops.</p>

<p>First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12738">influence voters’ responses</a> to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights. </p>

<p>This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “<a href="https://www.debate.com.mx/politica/elecciones-compra-de-votos-pan-nuevo-laredo-tamaulipas-ine-500-pesos-pintan-azul-rapan-desnudan-20180615-0130.html">Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos</a>.”  </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Supporters of the National Action Party (PAN) wave blue and white flags at a rally for their candidate, Ricardo Anaya, in February 2018." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767112/original/file-20261019-50-ljhnc8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767112/original/file-20261019-50-ljhnc8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=394&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767112/original/file-20261019-50-ljhnc8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=394&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767112/original/file-20261019-50-ljhnc8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=394&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767112/original/file-20261019-50-ljhnc8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=495&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767112/original/file-20261019-50-ljhnc8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=495&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767112/original/file-20261019-50-ljhnc8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=495&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In Mexico’s 2018 election, the PAN party, whose flags are pictured here, ran into opposition in Nuevo Laredo due to its vote-buying attempts.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Mexico%20Election/52b1854da39040d68ae944d959bc115f/photo">AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0010414020919919">moving targets</a>: Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision.</p>

<p>Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret. </p>

<p>It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment.</p>

<p>Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it.    </p>

<h2>Bringing it home</h2>

<p>Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely.</p>

<p>Partisanship, a <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691213453/the-bitter-end?srsltid=AU7gw4UfYZZRt2EyVlynbvVbLZcvebKX4rxNn2ZQuGWMGnL4kKDfpHLd">core element that makes people resistant</a> to vote buying, is very strong <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691213453/the-bitter-end?srsltid=AU7gw4UfYZZRt2EyVlynbvVbLZcvebKX4rxNn2ZQuGWMGnL4kKDfpHLd">in the U.S. electorate</a>. There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/poll-voters-say-trump-hurt-economy-competitive-midterm-election-looms-rcna597868">committed Democrats</a> will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism. </p>

<p>The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.” </p>

<p>At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vote to Republican. </p>

<p>In theory, there is one way Trump’s offer could succeed. Research shows that <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-political-science/article/machine-works-why-turnout-buying-is-more-effective-than-it-appears/5EDD14CB19A58C452663D4927BA30F5B">buying turnout, rather than trying to change vote choices, is routinely effective</a>. But all the examples come from countries where party officials actively monitor who comes to the polls. Without that surveillance, which is illegal in the U.S., the free-rider problem could bedevil turnout as well. </p>

<p>But whether enacted or not, the promise of cash for votes has a big downside for democracy. It means that no one will know whether victorious Republican candidates won this November because Americans preferred their policies and gave them a mandate – or because they expected to get paid.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293259/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Kenneth Greene&#39;s research has been funded by the National Science Foundation, the University of Texas at Austin, and the Mellon Foundation.</span></em></p></content>

<title>El Niño is threatening California’s fragile coast again – the 1982-83 El Niño opened eyes to the serious erosion risks</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763186/original/file-20260930-60-6o4qsq.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C8%2C1074%2C716&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Storm waves eroded the dunes from beneath homes in Pajaro Dunes, Calif., on Monterey Bay, during the powerful 1982-83 El Nino.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Gary Griggs</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>California’s coastal bluffs and beaches look rugged, but they can be surprisingly fragile in the face of a powerful El Niño.</p>

<p>The state saw that in 1982-83, when storms amid <a href="https://journals.flvc.org/jcr/article/view/80923/78067">one of the most destructive El Niño winters</a> in California history battered the coastline with powerful waves and torrential rain, leaving <a href="https://www.coastal.ca.gov/climate/extreme-weather/el-nino/">hundreds of millions of dollars in damage</a> in its wake. The storms coincided with elevated sea levels, high astronomical tides and very large waves delivered by repeated storms.</p>

<p>Extreme waves that winter destroyed <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_TmCGTQPyYw">one-third of the Santa Monica Pier</a> and tore off large sections of the Huntington Beach Pier and the Paradise Cove Pier, while <a href="https://www.surfer.com/news/super-el-nino-1983-california-coast-video">also damaging</a> the Seal Beach, San Clemente and Malibu piers. Numerous <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P5M8zVJDzTI">seawalls, decks and stairways</a> were torn apart, and 33 oceanfront homes were destroyed. </p>

<p>Massive waves also stripped millions of cubic yards of sand from Southern California beaches, and sections of the Pacific Coast Highway suffered severe flooding, mudslides and washouts.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>Along the central coast, <a href="https://doi.org/10.2112/JCOASTRES-D-25A-00003.1">waves and high-tide flooding eroded bluffs</a>. In Pacifica, just outside San Francisco, the edge of a sandy cliff lost over 65 feet as it failed, collapsing onto the beach and forcing the relocation of a two-story building and removal of an entire row of mobile homes. This area of high but <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t80GUlJDW_o">weak bluffs continued to erode</a> over the subsequent decades, forcing the demolition of bluff-top homes and apartments.</p>

<p>The El Niño now building in 2026-27 is <a href="https://iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/forecasts/enso/current/">forecast to be even stronger</a>, and coastal homes are <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/18/california-beach-erosion-san-clemente">already seeing damage</a>. I have studied <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=PCczXC0AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">coastal geology and oceanography</a> in California for nearly six decades. With the conditions expected this year, coastal flooding, coastal erosion and landslides are likely, and more dramatic cliff collapses wouldn’t be a surprise, though every El Niño is different.</p>

<h2>What is El Niño and why is it so destructive?</h2>

<p>El Niño is <a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html">one end of a climate pattern</a> that swings from warm to cold every few years and <a href="https://theconversation.com/2026s-el-nino-is-shaping-up-to-be-a-doozy-its-already-affecting-global-shipping-fish-behavior-and-heat-291490">can change weather patterns</a> around the world. Normally dry areas can experience flooding rains, and wet areas can suffer droughts. The <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/living-with-the-changing-california-coast/paper">U.S. Pacific Coast</a> in particular can take a beating from powerful atmospheric river storms with heavy downpours.</p>

<p><a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html">El Niños begin</a> with a shift in wind patterns, which normally push warm waters from east to west along the equator. For reasons still not fully understood, the trade winds die and the warm pool of water in the western Pacific begins to flow back toward the coast of South America.</p>



<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/WPA-KpldDVc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">What is El Niño? Met Office.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Part of this warm mass moves north toward the coast of California as a pulse or bulge, known as a Kelvin wave, and it begins to have far-ranging impacts.</p>

<p>Seawater expands as it warms, which <a href="https://sealevel.nasa.gov/sea-level-101/global-sea-level-rise/dive-deeper/">raises sea level</a> along the Pacific Coast for weeks during these periodic events. While all El Niños are not created equal, during the very large 1982-83 event, sea levels were elevated above predicted high tides by <a href="https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/map/">about a foot in San Diego to nearly 2 feet in San Francisco</a>.</p>

<p>These higher sea levels can reach higher elevations and last longer.</p>

Large slabs of the deck have fallen into the water." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763193/original/file-20260930-50-ywtuap.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763193/original/file-20260930-50-ywtuap.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763193/original/file-20260930-50-ywtuap.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763193/original/file-20260930-50-ywtuap.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763193/original/file-20260930-50-ywtuap.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=630&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763193/original/file-20260930-50-ywtuap.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=630&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763193/original/file-20260930-50-ywtuap.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=630&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>The elevated sea levels also allow storm waves to break closer to the shoreline, <a href="https://jcr.kglmeridian.com/view/journals/coas/42/5/article-p926.xml">eroding beaches and bluffs</a>, leading to damage and destruction of both private oceanfront development and public infrastructure, including streets and highways, bridges and piers, and parks and recreational facilities.</p>

<h2>Why California is vulnerable</h2>

<p>Much of California’s coastal and shoreline development took place from the late 1940s to the late 1970s when the state’s population exploded.</p>

<p>Homes were built on beaches, bluffs and dunes during a period when the <a href="https://jcr.kglmeridian.com/downloadpdf/view/journals/coas/41/5/article-p892.pdf">coastal storm climate was generally mild</a> and there were no real concerns with coastal hazards and future sea-level rise.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763194/original/file-20260930-60-6zinhp.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Condo buildings right at the edge of a cliff." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763194/original/file-20260930-60-6zinhp.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763194/original/file-20260930-60-6zinhp.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=882&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763194/original/file-20260930-60-6zinhp.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=882&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763194/original/file-20260930-60-6zinhp.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=882&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763194/original/file-20260930-60-6zinhp.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1108&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763194/original/file-20260930-60-6zinhp.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1108&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763194/original/file-20260930-60-6zinhp.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1108&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">The piers beneath these buildings on the cliff at Capitola, Calif., had little left to stand on after erosion from fierce El Niño-fueled storms.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>This changed quickly in <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/living-with-the-changing-california-coast/paper">1978 when the first strong El Niño</a> in recent memory arrived, raising alarm about the hazards ocean development was exposed to.</p>

<p>The extreme 1982-83 El Niño that followed a few years later caused about <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/living-with-the-changing-california-coast/paper">US$328 million (in 2025 dollars) in damage</a> to oceanfront property, $87 million in losses to recreational facilities such as piers, parking lots and access stairs, and $66 million in damage to large engineering structures such as breakwaters and jetties designed to protect harbors from storm waves.</p>

<p>At least in the short term, the 1982-83 El Niño winter <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/living-with-the-changing-california-coast/paper">changed popular perceptions</a> of the stability or security of oceanfront homes and other shoreline development. Building restrictions were tightened, insurance rates rose, and many requests for new seawall permits were submitted.</p>

<p>But then it was back to business as usual, as new arrivals to the coast outbid each other for the same oceanfront homes damaged a few years before.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/lEEQNlUXI4M?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Gary Griggs talks about erosion risks in the Santa Cruz area at the Seymour Marine Discovery Center.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/34843">Increased coastal armoring</a>, such as seawalls and <a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/seawalls-bulkheads-and-revetments.htm">rock revetments</a>, helped limit erosion during other very large El Niños that followed, <a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/billions/reports/19971201-19980228-severe-storm/tr9802.pdf">in 1997-98</a> and <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/publications/impacts-20152016-el-nino-californias-sandy-beaches">2015-16</a>, along with lucky timing that large waves arrived at low points in the monthly tidal cycle, leading to significantly less <a href="https://journals.flvc.org/jcr/article/view/80923/78067">property damage than in 1982-83</a>.</p>

<p>The coast was not so fortunate in <a href="https://jcr.kglmeridian.com/downloadpdf/view/journals/coas/41/5/article-p892.pdf">winter 2022-23</a>, when high seas and waves alone caused an estimated $4.7 billion in economic losses along California’s coast. The simultaneous occurrence of large storm waves, high tides and elevated sea levels were almost identical to the El Niño conditions in early 1983, 40 years earlier. </p>

<p>The state’s <a href="https://climateassessment.ca.gov/">latest climate assessment</a>, released Oct. 19, 2026,  warns of more intense storms and increased erosion as temperatures increase and sea level continues to rise.</p>

<h2>The El Niño of 2026-27</h2>

<p>What will California see in 2026-27?</p>

<p>The southern end of the state is already suffering wave damage from an <a href="https://theconversation.com/california-is-taking-a-beating-from-an-unusually-destructive-2026-pacific-hurricane-season-294207">exceptionally busy Pacific hurricane season</a>, also fueled by El Niño. Swells have <a href="https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-26/hurricane-polo-southern-california-waves">stripped away beaches and destroyed homes near San Diego</a>. The state’s storm season, when powerful atmospheric rivers bring downpours, typically begins in October or November and runs through early spring.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/precip/CWlink/MJO/enso.shtml">magnitude of the emerging 2026-27 El Niño</a>, likely to be one of the strongest on record, is making clear that coastal communities need to adapt now to a very different future.</p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Pacific Ocean waves generated by Hurricane Marie crash over a seawall protecting homes in Long Beach, Calif., on Sept. 7, 2026. El Nino’s warm water was already fueling powerful storms in the Pacific.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-an-aerial-view-people-gather-and-keep-watch-at-beachside-news-photo/2294090187">Mario Tama/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>How each coastal neighborhood, city and county responds will vary depending upon their local conditions and vulnerability to coastal erosion and flooding.</p>

<p>While many communities are stockpiling sandbags, clearing culverts and preparing evacuation plans, there are <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/48853095">limits on what they can do to stop erosion</a>. Building <a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/seawalls-bulkheads-and-revetments.htm">seawalls and rock revetments</a> can provide some protection if well designed, but they can also <a href="https://www.santacruzsentinel.com/2023/02/11/gary-griggs-our-ocean-backyard-seacliff-state-beach-wall-failures-continue/">create new problems</a>, including leading to the loss of beaches over time as sea levels continue to rise. Putting more sand on beaches is costly and very short-lived.</p>

<p>Extensive shoreline development, eroding bluffs, aging infrastructure and increasing exposure to extreme weather are placing growing pressure on coastal communities and shorelines around the world. Some will eventually face the difficult transition from continued shoreline protection to retreating from the coast – either planned retreat or following repeated damage. </p>

<p>There is little that any developed coastal area can do at this point to <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/w13162151">minimize the impacts</a> of the El Niño underway. What they can do is prepare to manage the risks and try to <a href="https://doi.org/10.2112/JCOASTRES-D-26TM4-00001.1">adapt to the changing future</a>.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293298/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767350/original/file-20261020-50-ag8pfj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4077%2C2718&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">International policing or international suppression of human rights?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/man-walk-past-a-billboard-for-the-signing-ceremony-high-news-photo/2242589324">Nhac Nguyen/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://www.unodc.org/roseap/en/2025/10/cybercrime-convention/story.html">United Nations Convention against Cybercrime</a> is the first international treaty aimed at combating criminal acts committed online and at supporting victims of those crimes. At the initial signing ceremony on Oct. 25, 2025, U.N. Secretary General António Guterres <a href="https://www.un.org/sg/en/content/sg/statements/2025-10-25/secretary-generals-remarks-the-cybercrime-convention-signing-ceremony-delivered">said the convention</a> was “a promise that fundamental human rights such as privacy, dignity and safety must be protected both offline and online.”</p>

<p>Civil society groups around the world, however, argue that the convention could make it easier for authoritarian governments to share information about people engaging in regular online activities. Because of vague language in the document, critics contend that governments would have the ability to <a href="https://www.accessnow.org/press-release/joint-statement-cybercrime-treaty-concluding-session/">criminalize legitimate online expression or other activities</a>. Legal gray areas also heighten concerns for the protection of whistleblowers, activists, journalists, researchers and others who could be targeted by governments known to restrict civil and political rights. </p>

<p>Nations have until Dec. 31, 2026, to sign the convention. It will enter into force after 40 signatory states become parties to it by ratifying it at home. As of October 2026, <a href="https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/cybercrime/convention/home.html">95 nations had signed the treaty</a>, but only three have become parties to it.</p>

<p>When the convention was being drafted, the Biden administration signaled its support <a href="https://usun.usmission.gov/explanation-of-position-of-the-united-states-on-the-adoption-of-the-resolution-on-the-un-convention-against-cybercrime-in-ungas-third-committee/">but acknowledged the concerns about potential misuse</a>. The U.S. has not signed the agreement. The Trump administration has said it will <a href="https://hanoiconvention.org/statement/united-states-of-americas-statement/">continue to consider the convention</a>. The administration has focused on promoting the United States’ own capabilities of combating cybercrime and has expressed concern about emboldening countries such as Russia and China to <a href="https://hanoiconvention.org/statement/united-states-of-americas-statement/">suppress freedom of expression and violate treaty obligations</a>.</p>

<p>We are <a href="https://www.meridithlavelle.com">political scientists</a> <a href="https://marylind23.github.io/website/">who study</a> human rights and digital repression. Human rights organizations globally are worried that authoritarian regimes could use the convention to attack researchers, journalists, human rights advocates and people who criticize governments. A day before the convention was signed, 19 nongovernmental organizations <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/10/24/joint-statement-on-the-signing-of-the-un-convention-on-cybercrime">released a joint statement</a> urging nations to not sign or ratify the treaty. Groups such as <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/12/30/new-un-cybercrime-treaty-primed-abuse">Human Rights Watch</a>, <a href="https://freedomhouse.org/article/freedom-house-urges-un-member-states-refrain-signing-un-convention-against-cybercrime">Freedom House</a>, <a href="https://www.accessnow.org/arab-region-cybercrime-laws-infringe-human-rights/?tztc=1">Access Now</a>, <a href="https://www.article19.org/resources/un-cybercrime-convention-a-blueprint-for-human-rights-violations/">Article 19</a> and others have warned that the convention’s human rights safeguards are inefficient. Weak protections risk further increases in transnational repression and global surveillance. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/eDYVUe8dPtI?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The Electronic Frontier Foundation is among the organizations that oppose the U.N. Convention against Cybercrime.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>



<h2>Verifying compliance is unclear</h2>

<p>Every country has its own domestic law enforcement system. And while there is no international government to enforce U.N. treaties, U.N. conventions are designed to help fill this gap. They <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2010357">rely on cooperation</a> among countries that have ratified an agreement by incorporating legal features to promote compliance. </p>

<p>When governments go through the ratification process, they adopt policies at home that reflect a treaty’s contents. But domestic interpretations of international laws often vary, which can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/acrefore/9780190846626.013.808">lead to patchy protection of human rights</a>. U.N. conventions on human rights also establish <a href="https://www.ohchr.org/en/core-international-human-rights-instruments-and-their-monitoring-bodies">treaty bodies</a>. They provide ways for independent experts to monitor human rights violations across all ratifying countries and to encourage more governments to join various conventions. These and other experts also participate in a process called the <a href="https://www.ohchr.org/en/hr-bodies/upr/upr-home">Universal Periodic Review</a>, in which countries examine the human rights records of other countries every 4.5 years and provide recommendations for improvement.</p>

<p>Although the U.N. cybercrime convention says that human rights must be respected, it is ultimately not a human rights treaty. It falls under the <a href="https://www.unodc.org/">U.N. Office of Drugs and Crime</a>. Because of this, there is no treaty body to monitor violations, making abuses that fall outside of regular law enforcement activities even more difficult to track. Some examples include <a href="https://ifex.org/egypt-judicial-authorities-employ-mass-surveillance-to-censor-citizens/">monitoring social media accounts of NGOs or activists</a>, remotely <a href="https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/IDAN/2022/732268/IPOL_IDA(2022)732268_EN.pdf">installing spyware onto journalists’ cellphones and other devices</a>, and <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/08/argentina-unchecked-deployment-of-ai-driven-surveillance-reinforces-a-techno-authoritarian-infrastructure-of-social-control/">using AI technologies against protesters and marginalized groups</a>. </p>

<p>The convention does say that ratifying countries will meet periodically to <a href="https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/cybercrime/convention/home.html">improve cooperation and review implementation</a>, but there are no stated goals about monitoring cybercrime or compliance with the convention. Another issue, which is present in all international laws, is <a href="https://legal.un.org/ilc/sessions/62/pdfs/english/guide_to_practice_reservations.pdf">treaty reservations</a>, which allow governments to effectively ratify treaties while <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0022002714567947">opting out of certain parts of them</a>. The three countries that have ratified the convention as of October 2026 — Vietnam, Qatar and Azerbaijan — did not stipulate any reservations.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/gXHfwqyhOu4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">International technology policy expert Nick Ashton-Hart discusses the origins of and issues with the U.N. Convention against Cybercrime.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Infringing on human rights</h2>

<p>Monitoring how governments comply with the cybercrime convention is critical to ensuring that governments do not infringe on human rights. International NGOs, domestic civil society organizations, journalists and other human rights defenders often work to scrutinize and share information on government abuses. Some governments see such work <a href="https://www.ohchr.org/en/special-procedures/sr-human-rights-defenders/challenges-faced-human-rights-defenders">as a threat</a>, and they often repress them. </p>

<p>There has also been a steady rise in governments <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/06/25/un-human-rights-office-calls-for-action-on-transnational-repression">repressing people outside of their borders</a>. Many governments <a href="https://ifex.org/last-year-saw-23-governments-engage-in-transnational-repression-to-silence-critics/">are doing this</a> through surveillance, monitoring social media, <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-doxxing-and-why-is-it-so-scary-95848">doxxing</a>, creating AI deepfakes and even forcibly repatriating critics in exile and imprisoning them. </p>

<p>Because the cybercrime convention promotes information sharing among ratifying countries, human rights organizations are concerned that governments with bad human rights records might use shared information and cooperation to arrest human rights defenders or anybody accused of what the governments label as a serious crime. The convention does not limit the use of these powers to the <a href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2023/09/uns-cybercrime-convention-draft-slippery-slope-lgbtq-and-gender-rights">set of core cybercrimes</a> it has defined, nor does it set a standard for what it considers to be a serious crime. </p>

<p>Instead, it allows countries to determine for themselves what constitutes a serious crime under domestic law. In many countries, this includes activities protected under international law, such as <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/10/24/joint-statement-on-the-signing-of-the-un-convention-on-cybercrime">criticism of the government, peaceful protest, same-sex relationships, investigative journalism and whistleblowing</a>. This puts vulnerable groups at risk. For example, in countries where it is illegal to share LGBTQ+ content online, a government could activate the surveillance measures outlined in the convention to track and target community members at home and abroad <a href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2023/09/uns-cybercrime-convention-draft-slippery-slope-lgbtq-and-gender-rights">under the guise of enforcing domestic law</a>. </p>

<p>Secretary General Guterres said at the signing ceremony that “<a href="https://www.un.org/sg/en/content/sg/statements/2025-10-25/secretary-generals-remarks-the-cybercrime-convention-signing-ceremony-delivered?_gl=1*1c7w33x*_ga*MTc2MzM5NjQyOS4xNzU5NjI4ODg5*_ga_S5EKZKSB78*czE3NjQxNzM1NTkkbzckZzEkdDE3NjQxNzQxNDYkajYwJGwwJGgw*_ga_TK9BQL5X7Z*czE3NjQxNzM1NTkkbzExJGcwJHQxNzY0MTczNTU5JGo2MCRsMCRoMA">in cyberspace, nobody is safe until everybody is safe</a>.” As countries consider ratifying the convention, we believe it would be wise to consider whether the agreement falls short of keeping people safe in cyberspace, and whether it might put human rights defenders, journalists, researchers and others in danger.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/269794/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Horror’s monsters find new meaning with queer and trans audiences – how ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ dissects identity</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767234/original/file-20261020-60-hca1rj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7421%2C4947&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">In &#39;Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,&#39; queer people watch themselves watch horror.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://mubi.com/en/us/films/teenage-sex-and-death-at-camp-miasma">MUBI</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Queer horror is having a moment. The recent film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt39143902">Leviticus</a>” (2026), a harrowing <a href="https://www.out.com/film/leviticus-adrian-chiarella-interview">allegory for conversion therapy</a>, was a critical hit. Meanwhile, Ryan Murphy’s <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/article/648149">undeniably gay</a> “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1844624/">American Horror Story</a>” returned to TV this fall, offering a <a href="https://www.wussymag.com/all/ahs-apocalypse-is-for-the-gays">campier approach</a> to the genre.</p>

<p>But queer people’s fascination with horror is by no means new. For trans and queer viewers, <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/distributed/Q/bo208655516.html">horror has long acted as a mirror</a> to reflect on complex personal questions of identity and embodiment.</p>

<p>Another new film, Jane Schoenbrun’s “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt35298123/">Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma</a>” (2026), explores queer people’s relationship with horror. Schoenbrun’s film isn’t really a horror movie; it’s a <a href="https://theconversation.com/teenage-sex-and-death-at-camp-miasma-winks-and-blows-a-blood-soaked-kiss-at-horror-films-of-queer-past-291752">movie about horror movies</a>. The protagonist, a young auteur named Kris, is rebooting an old slasher franchise, “Camp Miasma.” The franchise has aged poorly, and she wants to update the film for a contemporary audience. “This part’s transphobic!” Kris mutters while watching the original film.</p>

<p>But Kris is also helplessly obsessed with “Camp Miasma,” and Schoenbrun’s film suggests that it’s precisely the slasher’s troubling, problematic elements that have enthralled her. As both a trans studies scholar and a longtime horror fan, I know how she feels. In fact, Kris’ complicated relationship with “Camp Miasma” may feel deeply familiar for many queer and trans viewers.</p>

<p>Horror has produced some of the most objectionable queer- and trans-coded characters in cinema history. These portrayals of LGBTQ+ people as <a href="https://theconversation.com/teenage-sex-and-death-at-camp-miasma-winks-and-blows-a-blood-soaked-kiss-at-horror-films-of-queer-past-291752">monstrous and pathological</a> can be found in films ranging from the low-budget slashers that inspired Schoenbrun – most notably “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0086320/">Sleepaway Camp</a>” (1983) – to Oscar winners such as “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0102926/">The Silence of the Lambs</a>” (1991). </p>

<p>Yet queer and trans audiences have often <a href="http://feministing.com/2016/03/10/my-auntie-buffalo-bill-the-unavoidable-transmisogyny-of-silence-of-the-lambs/">found themselves strangely</a> <a href="https://feministpress.org/products/9781952177798-it-came-from-the-closet">drawn to these films</a> and to the <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/uncanny-valley-girls-zefyr-lisowski?variant=43555228287010">horror genre overall</a>. </p>

<p>Why does a genre that has treated LGBTQ+ people so poorly keep them coming back?</p>

<hr>

<h2>Horror against heteronormativity</h2>

<p>Queerness is baked into the very structure of the horror genre.</p>

<p>Film scholar Robin Wood summarized the <a href="https://doi.org/10.5749/j.ctvtv937f.9">horror formula</a> as “Normality is threatened by the Monster.” As Wood points out, the social order that represents “normality” is often tied to heteronormative structures like <a href="https://doi.org/10.63478/BLKRX8N4">the nuclear family</a> and the heterosexual couple. </p>

<p>Horror stages gleeful attacks on this order: Think of the family under siege by malevolent spirits, or the straight camp counselors hacked to bits after having sex. </p>

<p>Such themes may resonate strongly for queers who find their goals and desires in tension with a society primarily built around cisgender, heterosexual life paths.</p>

<h2>Body horror</h2>

<p>Beyond its social elements, horror also offers queer and trans people a personal encounter with an aspect of themselves that they may find confusing or even upsetting: their bodies. </p>

<p>Feminist scholar Carol Clover argued that horror is a “<a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2928507">body genre</a>,” meaning it is intended to activate a bodily response in the viewer. Often, one of the ways horror elicits this physical response is through the visceral, violent onscreen deformation of bodies. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/JE90x8fswlM?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Slasher films are notoriously bloody.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In <a href="https://cup.columbia.edu/book/body-horror/9780231220965/">body horror</a>, the human body is depicted as an unruly, often disgusting and always vulnerable <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-whale-is-a-horror-film-that-taps-into-our-fear-of-fatness-197859">accumulation of flesh</a>, blood and guts. Such images can <a href="https://conversationalist.org/2022/10/04/it-came-from-the-closet-queer-reflections-on-horror-book-excerpt-in-my-skin/">mirror and affirm</a> the <a href="https://www.them.us/story/body-horror-gender-dysphoria-essay">difficult feelings</a> that many queer and trans folks have experienced with regard to embodiment, their distress surrounding the forms their bodies take or the desires they feel.</p>

<p>Horror’s depiction of monsters and monstrous bodies have allowed many queer and trans people to take ownership over their experiences of personal pain and social stigma. As trans theorist Susan Stryker put it, “I want to lay claim to the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1215/10642684-1-3-237">dark power of my monstrous identity</a> without using it as a weapon against others or being wounded by it myself.”</p>

<h2>Questioning identification</h2>

<p>Other queer and trans writers, however, have asked about the limits of identifying with monstrosity.</p>

<p>“How does building an identity on reclaiming the boogeyman <a href="https://lareviewofbooks.org/article/nightmares-worth-indulging-on-feminist-presss-it-came-from-the-closet/">affect the psyche</a>?” wonders critic Grace Byron. Horror, after all, centers on violence, brutality, fear and even death. Identifying with these forces might feel powerful in the moment, but it doesn’t necessarily help reckon with the real violence that led LGBTQ+ people to identify with them in the first place.</p>

<p>When <a href="https://newsroom.ucla.edu/stories/wesleigh-gates-horror-films-trans-studies-podcast">I teach horror</a>, my students and I talk about how we might approach some of the most transphobic figures in the horror canon. Instead of identifying with these “monsters,” we try to think critically about the conditions that created them. </p>

<p>Take the trans-coded serial killer Buffalo Bill, from “The Silence of the Lambs.” Scholar <a href="https://www.flowjournal.org/2020/06/in-praise-of-the-bad-silence/">Cael Keegan</a> argues that “The Silence of the Lambs” raises issues of state violence against transgender people. Similarly, scholar <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv333kv90.11">Grace Lavery</a> reads Buffalo Bill as a victim of <a href="https://theconversation.com/gender-affirming-care-has-a-long-history-in-the-us-and-not-just-for-transgender-people-201752">medical gatekeeping</a>, which bars lifesaving gender-related care from those who need it. </p>

<p>Rather than either rejecting characters like Buffalo Bill or embracing their monstrosity, queer viewers and their allies could instead ask what these characters show about the structural conditions that keep queer and trans people at the margins of society.</p>

<h2>‘Disidentifying’ with horror</h2>

<p>When my students approach horror, I encourage them to consider the strategy that queer theorist José Esteban Muñoz offers for minority groups engaging with harmful representations in dominant culture: <a href="https://www.upress.umn.edu/9780816630158/disidentifications/">disidentification</a>. For Muñoz, to “disidentify” means refusing to see yourself in images that degrade you, yet still finding ways of making those violent representations generative for your own thinking, dreaming and living.</p>

<p>“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is about disidentifying with horror. It acknowledges the harmful, long-standing transphobia of the genre. And it is also frank about the disturbing prevalence of sexual violence in horror, both onscreen and <a href="https://melmagazine.com/en-us/story/harvey-weinstein-the-burning">behind the scenes</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767250/original/file-20261020-50-9u3xx6.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Film still of a young girl in a dark room, sitting before a TV filled with static" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767250/original/file-20261020-50-9u3xx6.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767250/original/file-20261020-50-9u3xx6.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767250/original/file-20261020-50-9u3xx6.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767250/original/file-20261020-50-9u3xx6.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767250/original/file-20261020-50-9u3xx6.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767250/original/file-20261020-50-9u3xx6.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767250/original/file-20261020-50-9u3xx6.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>But the queer characters in “Camp Miasma” – both in Schoenbrun’s film and in its fictional counterpart – still manage to connect with themselves and their bodies. And I think they do this not just by watching horror, but by watching themselves watch horror.</p>

<p>So perhaps the draw of horror for queer and trans people isn’t just that it lets them identify with onscreen monsters or victims of violence. It’s that it gives them the opportunity to reflect on these identifications – and to reject them or transform them.</p>

<p>In the process of finding meaning in horror’s monstrous worlds, queer and trans people tap into their own power to respond to the monstrous world around them.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291766/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

excerpt: In 'Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,' queer people watch themselves watch horror
body: In 'Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,' queer people watch themselves watch horror
The recent film “ Leviticus ” (2026), a harrowing allegory for conversion therapy , was a critical hit
Meanwhile, Ryan Murphy’s undeniably gay “ American Horror Story ” returned to TV this fall, offering a campier approach to the genre
But queer people’s fascination with horror is by no means new
For trans and queer viewers, horror has long acted as a mirror to reflect on complex personal questions of identity and embodiment
Another new film, Jane Schoenbrun’s “ Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma ” (2026), explores queer people’s relationship with horror
Schoenbrun’s film isn’t really a horror movie; it’s a movie about horror movies

The protagonist, a young auteur named Kris, is rebooting an old slasher franchise, “Camp Miasma.” The franchise has aged poorly, and she wants to update the film for a contemporary audience. “This part’s transphobic!” Kris mutters while watching the original film
But Kris is also helplessly obsessed with “Camp Miasma,” and Schoenbrun’s film suggests that it’s precisely the slasher’s troubling, problematic elements that have enthralled her
As both a trans studies scholar and a longtime horror fan, I know how she feels
In fact, Kris’ complicated relationship with “Camp Miasma” may feel deeply familiar for many queer and trans viewers
Horror has produced some of the most objectionable queer- and trans-coded characters in cinema history

These portrayals of LGBTQ+ people as monstrous and pathological can be found in films ranging from the low-budget slashers that inspired Schoenbrun – most notably “ Sleepaway Camp ” (1983) – to Oscar winners such as “ The Silence of the Lambs ” (1991)
Yet queer and trans audiences have often found themselves strangely drawn to these films and to the horror genre overall
Why does a genre that has treated LGBTQ+ people so poorly keep them coming back? No one’s 20s and 30s look the same
You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent
You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare
No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone

Read more from Quarter Life: ‘Heartstopper’ is helping LGBTQ+ fans find hope and community across time and space Childhood experiences of LGBTQ+ stigma can harm romantic relationships decades later – psychologists explain how to reconnect with yourself and your partner Heated Rivalry shows how queer joy can disrupt hockey’s culture of masculinity Horror against heteronormativity Queerness is baked into the very structure of the horror genre

Film scholar Robin Wood summarized the horror formula as “Normality is threatened by the Monster.” As Wood points out, the social order that represents “normality” is often tied to heteronormative structures like the nuclear family and the heterosexual couple
Horror stages gleeful attacks on this order: Think of the family under siege by malevolent spirits, or the straight camp counselors hacked to bits after having sex
Such themes may resonate strongly for queers who find their goals and desires in tension with a society primarily built around cisgender, heterosexual life paths
Body horror Beyond its social elements, horror also offers queer and trans people a personal encounter with an aspect of themselves that they may find confusing or even upsetting: their bodies
Feminist scholar Carol Clover argued that horror is a “ body genre ,” meaning it is intended to activate a bodily response in the viewer
Often, one of the ways horror elicits this physical response is through the visceral, violent onscreen deformation of bodies
In body horror , the human body is depicted as an unruly, often disgusting and always vulnerable accumulation of flesh , blood and guts

Such images can mirror and affirm the difficult feelings that many queer and trans folks have experienced with regard to embodiment, their distress surrounding the forms their bodies take or the desires they feel
Horror’s depiction of monsters and monstrous bodies have allowed many queer and trans people to take ownership over their experiences of personal pain and social stigma

As trans theorist Susan Stryker put it, “I want to lay claim to the dark power of my monstrous identity without using it as a weapon against others or being wounded by it myself.” Questioning identification Other queer and trans writers, however, have asked about the limits of identifying with monstrosity. “How does building an identity on reclaiming the boogeyman affect the psyche ?” wonders critic Grace Byron
Horror, after all, centers on violence, brutality, fear and even death
Identifying with these forces might feel powerful in the moment, but it doesn’t necessarily help reckon with the real violence that led LGBTQ+ people to identify with them in the first place
When I teach horror , my students and I talk about how we might approach some of the most transphobic figures in the horror canon
Instead of identifying with these “monsters,” we try to think critically about the conditions that created them
Take the trans-coded serial killer Buffalo Bill, from “The Silence of the Lambs.” Scholar Cael Keegan argues that “The Silence of the Lambs” raises issues of state violence against transgender people
Similarly, scholar Grace Lavery reads Buffalo Bill as a victim of medical gatekeeping , which bars lifesaving gender-related care from those who need it

Rather than either rejecting characters like Buffalo Bill or embracing their monstrosity, queer viewers and their allies could instead ask what these characters show about the structural conditions that keep queer and trans people at the margins of society. ‘Disidentifying’ with horror When my students approach horror, I encourage them to consider the strategy that queer theorist José Esteban Muñoz offers for minority groups engaging with harmful representations in dominant culture: disidentification

For Muñoz, to “disidentify” means refusing to see yourself in images that degrade you, yet still finding ways of making those violent representations generative for your own thinking, dreaming and living. “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is about disidentifying with horror
It acknowledges the harmful, long-standing transphobia of the genre
And it is also frank about the disturbing prevalence of sexual violence in horror, both onscreen and behind the scenes
Watching monsters on screen provides an opportunity to forge new relationships to the monstrous world beyond it

title: Russia released a US prisoner. What did they get out of it?
excerpt: Donald Trump speaks during an RNC fundraising event at Mar-a-Lago on October 16, 2026. | Eric Lee/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily
body: Donald Trump speaks during an RNC fundraising event at Mar-a-Lago on October 16, 2026. | Eric Lee/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is cozying up to Russia again.  What’s happening? On Wednesday, Russia released an American prisoner , 74-year-old retired teacher Stephen Hubbard, back to the US
The US, Trump said in a social media post, “out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return.”  Hubbard’s release is unquestionably good news

But Trump is wrong: In just the last month, his administration has delivered for Russia in more ways than one, often inexplicably and despite bipartisan condemnation.  What is Trump doing for Russia? Late last week, he waived upcoming economic sanctions on Russia that he had only recently signed into law after they passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support

He also:  Struck a diesel deal with Russia, temporarily lifting fuel sanctions on the country in exchange for Russia releasing a trivial amount of diesel into the global market; Announced — seemingly without talking to either party — a Russia-Ukraine “energy ceasefire” favorable to Russia (which has since fallen apart); Temporarily interrupted US intel sharing with Ukraine and played a role in interfering with Ukraine’s access to Starlink, which helps power the country’s drone warfare against Russia; and Called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced
Last month, Trump also  invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the annual G20 summit later this year, which would mark Putin’s first appearance since 2019

What does Trump get out of all of this? There’s Hubbard’s release, but taking that on Trump’s own terms ( muddled though they are), the US didn’t give anything to secure it — which means that all of those favors have amounted to not much at all, other than papering over Russia’s role as an international bad actor and breaking with US allies in Europe.  Why does this matter? Trump’s Russia embrace comes at an awful time for Ukraine, which, as the New York Times reported earlier this month, is facing a Russian campaign to “freeze Ukrainians into submission” as winter approaches
Nevertheless, on Wednesday, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian.” And with that, it’s time to log off… I was delighted to learn about the US’s new national park yesterday, its 64th
Chiricahua National Park — until Tuesday, only a national monument — is the first new park in six years

Located in southeastern Arizona, it’s also called the “Wonderland of Rocks,” according to the Washington Post ; you can read more about it here with a gift link.  Have a great evening, and we’ll see you back here tomorrow!

body: On October 22, Vox is co-hosting a panel and reception honoring the 2o26 L’Oréal-UNESCO for Women in Science 2026 Award recipients, our second year celebrating this group of scientists
The program, part of the global L’Oréal-UNESCO for Women in Science initiative, recognizes five women postdoctoral scientists whose research ranges from bioengineering to astronomy

Danielle Stevens: Innate Immunity, Computational Biology — University of California, Berkeley Using artificial intelligence to speed up the engineering of disease-resistant crops by targeting plant immune receptors, with the goal of cutting global pesticide use and protecting our food supply

Anna Romanov: Bioengineering: Immunology — Massachusetts Institute of Technology Integrating bioengineering, synthetic biology, and immunology to build molecular technologies that reveal how B-cells evolve, then applying those insights to the development of vaccines and biologic therapies

Katherine Lagerstrom: Ecology and Evolutionary Biology — Princeton University Studying how human-driven change — pollution, antibiotics, captivity, and human contact — reshapes animal microbiomes and the way microbes evolve, including the spread of antibiotic resistance in the gut microbiome

Clarissa Do Ó: Astronomy & Planetary Sciences — California Institute of Technology (Caltech) Building the tools and technologies used to photograph planets beyond our solar system, laying the groundwork for finding new Earth-like planets rotating around Sun-like stars to allow deeper understanding of where our own planet fits in the universe

Tana Pottorf: Neuroimmunology — The Ohio State University Investigating the role of immune cells (macrophages) after spinal cord injury, aiming to develop therapies that preserve their helpful effects while curbing chronic inflammation and improving recovery
