title: What Christina Applegate’s misdiagnosis reveals about MS
excerpt: Christina Applegate at the 2023 Screen Actors Guild awards. | Valerie Macon/AFP via Getty Images Christina Applegate, the actor who has been one of the most vis
body: Christina Applegate at the 2023 Screen Actors Guild awards. | Valerie Macon/AFP via Getty Images Christina Applegate, the actor who has been one of the most visible faces of multiple sclerosis since her 2021 diagnosis, made a stunning revelation this week: She does not have MS after all

And her doctors still don’t know what is causing her debilitating symptoms. “I’m back at square one,” Applegate told fellow actor Jamie Lynn Sigler, who does have MS, on Sigler’s podcast MeSsy . “I was not happy at all
Everybody else was so happy.” It is a harrowing predicament for Applegate, and hopefully her medical team is able to get her the diagnosis and treatment she needs
But the fact is, her experience is not unique
Even as more and more Americans get diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, misdiagnosis remains all too common
According to one meta-analysis, roughly 15 percent of MS diagnoses may actually be false positives

How could such a common medical condition — roughly 1 million Americans are living with the disease, about one in every 350 people — remain such a mystery? After Applegate’s announcement, I called some leading experts on MS to ask why diagnosing the disease is such a challenge, and what they want people to know

Why MS can be challenging to diagnose Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune condition: The body mistakenly attacks cells meant to protect your brain and spinal cord, and the resulting damage interrupts nerve signals and causes the disease’s telltale symptoms of motor impairment, tingling sensations, and vision problems
Some people experience a rollercoaster of relapses and remissions; others see the disease steadily progress, eventually leading to serious disability
The reality is, scientists still don’t really know what causes MS to develop, said Dr
Andrew Solomon , a neurologist at the University of Vermont who specializes in MS
Obesity and metabolic problems play a role, but we need more research

Even the precise role of genetics remains something of a mystery. “We don’t really know what causes or triggers the autoimmune response in any given individual,” Solomon said.  And that’s where the challenge in diagnosing it begins
First, the testing can be imprecise; there is not a single test that reliably diagnoses MS
If a doctor suspects their patient may have MS, they usually undergo an MRI, which their physicians then scour for lesions that are typically associated with the disease
But those scans are still subject to interpretation: Other rare conditions sometimes resemble MS in imaging, as can diseases of blood vessels in the brain
You can also receive a spinal fluid analysis to check for abnormalities in your immune system, which the vast majority of MS patients have
The nature of MS symptoms adds to the difficulty
They can often be vague early on: brain fog or fatigue or a general malaise

The tingling or vision problems can be similar to symptoms for other conditions that are not MS, and they are easily dismissed if they go into temporary remission, as often happens during the initial phases of the disease. “Neurological symptoms sometimes can be vague — numbness, pins and needles — and it’s usually short-lived,” Dr

Saud Sadiq , chief research scientist and director of the Tisch Multiple Sclerosis Research Center of New York, told me. “Unless they’re taken seriously initially, they may be ignored because by the time the patient goes through the healthcare system and is actually referred to a neurologist, the symptoms have abated.” If your doctor is diagnosing you with MS, ask directly: What’s the evidence? One 2025 study by Solomon and his colleagues found that 40 percent of people who had later been d iagnosed with multiple sclerosis were initially misdiagnosed with a different disease. “Because it’s so heterogeneous, it doesn’t present in the same way in everybody and can have varying severity, it can be hard to diagnose sometimes,” Solomon said
Lastly, when people are experiencing debilitating symptoms, there is pressure to deliver some diagnosis — and that may push some doctors to leap to MS even if they are not sure, Solomon said

The recent advent of effective treatments that help manage the disease’s symptoms, especially when it is caught early, may add to that pressure, even if the better course would be to continue monitoring the person before they start a medication. “There may be a lot of clinicians who, if they can’t find a better explanation than MS, may be inclined to diagnose MS, even if they don’t really meet our diagnostic criteria, because they’re worried about missing a window of opportunity to treat somebody,” Solomon said
There is reason to hope the MS misdiagnosis problem could get better

The National Multiple Sclerosis Society released new diagnostic criteria in 2024 that Solomon said more physicians should become familiar with to better distinguish MS from problems like migraines or vascular disease
And because imaging is involved in diagnosis, there is optimism that AI could be a powerful new tool in delivering more accurate results

What everyone should know about MS symptoms and diagnosis The good news is that MS, when diagnosed properly, is a treatable condition these days. “The prognosis with new drugs is extremely good for long-term care,” Sadiq told me. “If patients stick to treatment at a good MS center, you can look forward to a life without disability in 2026.” So it is worth being vigilant and talking to your doctor if you experience any concerning symptoms
You should seek care if you have numbness or pins and needles that persists for more than 24 to 48 hours, Sadiq said, or have motor problems, like one hand won’t work as you try to play piano

Annette Langer-Gould , who develops and evaluates programs for MS care at Kaiser Permanente, said numbness in your abdomen, chest or back, as opposed to your extremities, is a particular cause for concern

If one eye has normal vision and the other is blurred, that’s another good reason to get checked out.  If you do get tested, make sure the actual images of your MRIs end up being reviewed by an expert in MS. “The most common reasons the disease is still misdiagnosed are related to the providers’ lack of expertise usually in reading MRI scans,” Langer-Gould said
The spinal tap may sound scary, and doctors sometimes don’t recommend them because their insurance reimbursement is low — but they add to the confidence of a diagnosis
They are worth it, she said. “American patients are very afraid of the spinal tap,” Langer-Gould said. “My message to patients is: Listen, just get the spinal
This way we’ll be sure.” And do not be afraid to seek a second opinion for such a serious diagnosis, Sadiq added

If your doctor is diagnosing you with MS, ask directly: What’s the evidence? If your doctor is recommending that you start treatment, it could also be worth checking whether they have a relationship with a pharmaceutical company that affects how you perceive their judgment, Langer-Gould said
People who have already been diagnosed may also be shaken by the Applegate news and question whether their own diagnosis might be wrong
Solomon said that folks should have a frank conversation with their physician about how exactly their case met the diagnostic criteria
With proper imaging and the spinal fluid tests, you can get to a confident diagnosis for the vast majority of people
But be your own advocate to make sure you’re satisfied. “For many people, the diagnosis actually can be very straightforward,” Solomon said. “We really have no question about what it is.”

title: This Democrat’s accountability plan has Trump fuming
excerpt: Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) at a news conference in the US Capitol on June 18, 2026. | Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The 2026 midterms are less than
body: Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) at a news conference in the US Capitol on June 18, 2026. | Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The 2026 midterms are less than two weeks away, which means we’ll soon have a better idea of what the next two years of American politics could look like
If Democrats win at least one chamber of Congress — and they’re comfortable favorites to control the House — they’ll enter 2027 with oversight power for the first time in Donald Trump’s second term
If they win the Senate, too, they’ll have even more power.  Whatever the outcome, Michigan Sen
Elissa Slotkin wants her party to hit the ground running

In an interview with Vox’s Astead Herndon at the University of Chicago’s Institute of Politics , she explained that the key divide in the Democratic Party is no longer “moderate versus progressive.”  “Particularly in the era of Trump, I think it is fight versus flight,” she said. “Regardless of your persuasion, do you believe that we need to think differently about how we exercise power and oversight in the era of Trump and if we don’t, we’re at risk of losing our country as we know it?”  Slotkin, who says she’s on “Team Fight,” discusses what that Day 1 Democratic agenda should look like, how she plans to hold the Trump administration accountable, whether she’s considering a presidential bid, and more
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel

How does Congress reassert its role so that people believe in the kind of checks and balances that Trump has washed away? When I think about, hopefully, Democrats doing well in a few short weeks here, the election is the end of one phase, but a much more important phase then comes into focus, and that’s what you do with the power that you’ve won
If we manage to win the House and especially the House and the Senate, there’s three things that we need to do
One, we need to pick two or three big pieces of legislation that speak directly to people’s pocketbooks and go hard on those — I would say housing and healthcare
Number two, we do have to have accountability for the unbelievable corruption that we are living under right now
But you can’t just make that your whole personality
You have to pick signature cases, and you have to go after people and projects that are super egregious
Everyone knows the East Wing of the White House, and people feel that in a way that’s different from a nameless contract at the Pentagon or whatever
So you need to pick those signature cases and go hard on accountability, not just Trump

Because of course, there will be moments of, “Let’s go after Trump himself.” As someone who voted to impeach him twice, he’s still there, right? But the people around Donald Trump who are doing his bidding and enabling this have no such immunity
They have no immunity the way the president does
And to me, he couldn’t do any of this stuff without all of those people saluting and supporting it

So you go after the people who do his bidding.  Third, we have to Trump-proof the government going forward so that no president of any party can ever abuse the system the way he did, because we figured out under Trump that a lot of the stuff that we thought were laws were actually just norms, standards, habits, expectations, good citizens
And when you have a president who has no shame, they just walk all over that
And then even for things that were laws, the penalties, the teeth are not there
So you make an ad that plays during a football game, a political ad paid for by US taxpayer dollars, your dollars
The penalty is like, you have to pay a fine
Well, if they have the money and they have all the keys to the government, they’re going to pay that fine and not worry about it
So how do we get teeth in the things that were laws and strengthen those other laws going forward? You mentioned Trump-proofing the government
At this point, he has stacked the courts with a lot of favorable folks
He controls the Republican Party, has installed people who do his bidding on each of those levels
Is that possible? It does seem a little hard to figure out how the government becomes Trump-proof when it’s beyond an individual at this point
One of the things I think is changing about politics is that there is a groundswell of energy around certain issues that is not partisan
The groundswell going on in the Midwest about data centers or Flock cameras or AI in general is not like, “I’m a Democrat, I’m a Republican.” It is organized and grassroots
Data centers went zero to 60 faster than any issue I’ve seen out there
And I think harnessing that outrage — and that outrage also, I think, is growing on the corruption side — so how do you harness that for an ethics package?  And look, I don’t agree with Sen
Josh Hawley of Missouri on almost anything, but he has a bill to get rid of corporate PACs and money in politics
Working with strange bedfellows, I think there is still a lot we can do because of that upward pressure

The other piece I was going to ask about — you mentioned the impeachment efforts, and I feel like one of the things that came from those was a lack of belief from the public about the effectiveness of those efforts
Let’s say Democrats were to take back the House and possibly the Senate
Should impeachment be a focus of a potentially incoming Democratic House? I will say, because I still see him on the floor, that if Sen
Mitch McConnell had done the right thing, then Donald Trump would have been impeached after January 6, but he did not
And his legacy, along with his health issues, will be how he is remembered
I am into effectiveness, and if we have the House but not the Senate, I don’t have a ton of faith that my Republican colleagues are going to have any more strength

title: The Supreme Court may be about to make America’s prisons much crueler
excerpt: Update, October 21, 11:45 am ET: The Supreme Court released a brief order on October 21, which ruled against the Trump administration’s request to deny gender-a
body: Update, October 21, 11:45 am ET: The Supreme Court released a brief order on October 21, which ruled against the Trump administration’s request to deny gender-affirming care to transgender prisoners
And it does not explain the Court’s reasoning
So it is not clear why the Court ruled against Trump or even whether Trump will lose if this case reaches the Court again after it has be fully litigated in lower courts
Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented
The article below was originally published on October 13

On the first day of his second term, President Donald Trump issued an executive order requiring the Bureau of Prisons to “ensure that no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” Issued alongside a record 26 other orders that day, it was an unsurprising development, because Trump had made this issue one of the centerpieces of his 2024 campaign
The fate of that executive order, as well as the US Bureau of Prisons’ (“BOP”) memoranda implementing the order, is now before the Supreme Court in a case called Trump v

And, while this case obviously has high stakes for incarcerated transgender people specifically, the Court’s resolution of this case could potentially have far greater reach — cutting off many cis and transgender people’s access to healthcare while they are incarcerated
That’s because one of the central questions in Kingdom — though this issue is not yet before the justices — is when the Constitution requires prisons to provide medical care to incarcerated people

Gamble (1976), the Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment’s ban on “cruel and unusual punishments” imposes on the government an “obligation to provide medical care for those whom it is punishing by incarceration.” People in prison, after all, cannot simply drive themselves to the hospital if they get sick
If the prison does not give them adequate medical care, they will suffer untreated and potentially die
For procedural reasons, the Court is unlikely to opine on whether Estelle requires prisons to provide gender-affirming care to trans people right away

But the question of when the Eighth Amendment requires prisons to provide medical care to incarcerated people is front and center in the Kingdom case , which means the Court could potentially use Kingdom to limit all imprisoned people’s access to healthcare — or even to undercut the Constitution’s protections against cruel and unusual punishments more broadly
Ironically, this case also arises out of a famous political blunder by pro-trans advocates

Kamala Harris was seeking her party’s 2020 presidential nomination, the ACLU circulated a questionnaire to candidates that asked if they would use presidential authority “to ensure that transgender and nonbinary people who rely on the state for medical care — including those in prison and immigration detention — will have access to comprehensive treatment associated with gender transition, including all necessary surgical care?”  Harris responded that she would, and also said that she “pushed the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation to provide gender transition surgery to state inmates” while she was state attorney general.  Years later, during his 2024 debate with Harris, Trump claimed that the then-vice president “ wants to do transgender operations on illegal aliens that are in prison .” And not long after, his opposition to gender-affirming care for trans people in prison became a key part of his campaign
It’s unclear why the ACLU thought it was a good idea to shine a light on this issue in 2019 because, at the time, the BOP provided gender-affirming care to people in federal prison

The ACLU — which represents the pro-trans side in the Kingdom case — now argues that transgender people in federal prison have had access to at least some forms of gender-affirming care “ since at least 1992 .” Indeed, Trump’s own administration concluded in a 2018 memo that the Bureau of Prisons’ “statutory mandate to provide basic medical and mental health care” to incarcerated people obligated it to provide “pharmaceutical interventions (e.g., cross-gender hormone therapy), hair removal and surgery (if individualized assessment indicates surgical intervention is applicable)” to transgender people in prison if their doctors determined that these interventions are “medically necessary care.” In any event, regardless of why Trump fixated on cutting off trans healthcare for people in federal prison, Kingdom is now before the Court

That means that the fate of trans people in prison — and, if the Eighth Amendment issue eventually reaches the Court, all incarcerated people — is now in the hands of a Republican Court that is often hostile to trans litigants, and that has, at times, signaled that it wants to drastically roll back the scope of the Eighth Amendment
What are the legal issues in the Kingdom case? At least since Estelle , the Court has held that people who are incarcerated are not also sentenced to live and die without medical care

Plata (2011), “a prison that deprives prisoners of basic sustenance, including adequate medical care, is incompatible with the concept of human dignity and has no place in civilized society.” Under Estelle and Brown , transgender people often have a right to gender-affirming care during their incarceration
As the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held in Edmo v
Corizon (2019), such a person must show that they have a “serious medical need” for such care — typically by demonstrating that the care was prescribed to them by their health provider
But the Constitution does not permit prisons to deny medically necessary care to incarcerated people
In Kingdom , the ACLU raised this Eighth Amendment argument in the lower courts, but those lower courts ruled in favor of transgender people in prison on different, much more technical legal grounds

For over three decades, from at least 1992 to 2025, according to the ACLU’s brief to the justices , the BOP provided at least some gender-affirming care, including hormone therapy, to transgender people

This matters because, when a federal agency changes its policies, a federal law typically requires it to “ examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action , including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.” This explanation often must explain the agency’s justification for “disregarding facts and circumstances” that justified the previous policy

Both the ACLU and the lower courts that heard Kingdom argue that the Trump administration did not comply with this obligation when it cut off care for trans people in prison.  Among other things, the district court that heard this case determined that the administration cited “ zero evidence from its own medical or mental health care professionals to support its conclusions” against providing transgender healthcare

While the Trump administration argues that providing gender-affirming care makes prisons less safe, the district court also noted that “the government has not cited a single instance of gender-affirming care giving rise to safety concerns despite having provided such care for many years.” Is this a persuasive legal argument against the Trump administration’s new policy? I think it is
And so did three federal judges that previously heard the Kingdom case

But the fate of trans people in prison is now in the hands of a Supreme Court that rarely rules in favor of transgender litigants, and that has a history of handing down legally incoherent opinions that are inconsistent with the Court’s own precedents , and that also deny legal rights to trans people

The current Court’s uncertain commitment to the Eighth Amendment Because the lower courts that heard Kingdom did not rule on the Eighth Amendment question, Kingdom should not currently give the justices an opportunity to roll back Estelle

But, in the likely event that this Court rejects the ACLU’s argument that the Trump administration did not adequately explain its new policy, the case will return to the lower courts and the Eighth Amendment issue will be fully litigated — teeing up the Eighth Amendment question for the justices to decide in the near future

This issue could arise, moreover, at the exact moment that some justices are pushing for sweeping changes to how their Court understands the term “cruel and unusual punishments.” Indeed, at least some of the Supreme Court’s recent Eighth Amendment precedents suggest that the Republican justices want a wholesale rewrite of the Court’s previous precedents laying out what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment

Since the mid-to-late twentieth century, the Court has held that, in Chief Justice Earl Warren’s words, the Eighth Amendment “must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society .” Thus, as certain forms of punishment grow more uncommon, they become more constitutionally dubious
This “evolving standards of decency” framework is front and center in nearly every major Supreme Court decision interpreting the Eighth Amendment for the last five or six decades, including Estelle
Precythe (2019), however, the Court’s Republican majority seemed to abandon this framework

Although decades worth of pre -Bucklew decisions established that a punishment is unconstitutional if it is considered cruel and unusual today , Bucklew suggested that a method of punishment is unconstitutional only if it “had fallen out of use” at “the time of the founding.”  Bucklew did list some methods of punishment that fail this test, but they are things like “disemboweling” or “burning alive.”    Thus, if taken seriously, Bucklew ’s new approach to Eighth Amendment cases would dramatically expand the government’s power to impose harsh punishments

The late Justice Antonin Scalia, for example, argued that a Bucklew -like approach to the Eighth Amendment does not prohibit the government from executing most intellectually disabled offenders, and that it does not limit the government’s ability to impose excessive punishments for minor crimes
In fairness, some of the Court’s post- Bucklew decisions are inconsistent with the framework the Court laid out in that case
So at least some of the justices who joined Bucklew may have since decided that it’s a bad idea to toss out the Court’s entire framework for Eighth Amendment cases

title: You can now create an AI version of a dead loved one. Here’s what could happen.
excerpt: It’s now possible to create AI chatbots of loved ones to interact with after their death
body: It’s now possible to create AI chatbots of loved ones to interact with after their death

But that raises some difficult questions, like: If you do, how might the experience shape your grief?  This is one of the questions driving a global study of digital “deadbots” — AI models trained on a deceased person’s texts, voicemails, and other personal data

Through this work, researchers are exploring what it might mean that we can now use this emerging technology to talk to simulations of the dead.  In the latest episode of Unexplainable , I spoke with some of these researchers investigating the potential impacts of “postmortem avatars” on people who are grieving, on the legacies and rights of the deceased, and on grief practices around the world
Because while deadbots may feel unfamiliar, the impulse behind them is deeply relatable
In times of loss, isn’t this what many of us want — to continue conversations with the people we’re missing? I have experienced this longing in my own life
After two of my closest friends died around the same time, all I wanted, and all their families wanted, was to keep talking to them
I wrote a book, Other People’s Words , about sustaining relationships with people we’ve lost by continuing to engage with the language they leave behind

So when I heard about deadbots and the digital afterlife industry, I wanted to understand what researchers are learning about the role of AI in shaping conversations that carry forward after death.  One of these investigators is Katarzyna Nowaczyk-Basińska , an assistant professor at the University of Cambridge, who has been studying “digital immortality” for more than a decade

Among the questions she’s asking are: “Who is enabled to persist beyond death? In what form? Through which technologies? Under whose control?”  Deadbots over dinner  Researching AI with study subjects who are grieving is tricky
And asking them to engage with new software could be harmful

So, instead, Nowaczyk-Basińska teamed up with a death doula and traveled around the globe to convene a series of focus groups — in the format of intimate dinners — bringing together people with a range of experiences with grief to talk about life, death, and bots.  She recounts one event in which she spoke with a mother in Poland whose son had recently died. “One of the first things that she shared with us was that she feels that she’s ready to digitally resurrect her deceased son,” Nowaczyk-Basińska told me.  When Nowaczyk-Basińska hears something like this, she aims to listen and embrace where the person is coming from

The goal of the dinners is not to persuade people one way or another but to learn how people genuinely respond to what AI can do, and to understand how these tools might align or collide with local grief practices.  She chose specific locations for these gatherings — China, India, and Poland — to help address gaps in technology research, which tends to favor what behavioral scientists sometimes call the “ WEIRD ,” an acronym for “Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic.”  By the end of that dinner in Poland, the mother Nowaczyk-Basińska talked with came to a very different decision about creating a postmortem avatar of her son. “She realized that it might be helpful, but it also at the same time can add additional burdens… And it’s not her son,” Nowaczyk-Basińska says. “She realized that these technologies are part of the very, very big commercial market
And that the main goal of this market is to make better retention, better attachment, better mechanisms for monetization
So it’s not ‘care.’” To be fair, grief has always been a business, and people have been making money from it forever
Companies will try to upsell you on fancy gravestones or gold-plated coffins
But AI has the potential to fundamentally re-engineer our relationship to loss
In 2024, the “digital legacy industry” was valued at $22 billion, and it’s expected to grow to almost $80 billion by 2034

That number lumps new deadbot platforms in with much more widely used and established grief tech, like online memorials, counseling resources, and estate planning tools.  But deadbot usage is hard to track because you actually don’t need a special tool to create digital doubles of the deceased — though dedicated apps do already exist

At this point, you can feed simple prompts into a general-purpose AI chatbot and start interacting with a simulation of your lost loved one in a matter of minutes.  I know this because I tried it with my friend Christine, who died 11 years ago

Was this whole exercise a violation, since I know Christine hated technology? Which version of her should I even try to resurrect — the English teacher, the activist, the friend — the voice before or after she started to experience her early-onset dementia?  The ethical questions raised by deadbots are gnarly

And that’s one of the reasons Nowaczyk-Basińska, back when she was designing her study of digital immortality, invited a colleague of hers at Cambridge to join her research, one who focuses on AI ethics.  How to design a deadbot Tomasz Hollanek is a critical designer and AI ethicist, and he often uses a methodology called “speculative design.” In this approach, researchers come up with hypothetical scenarios based on existing technology trends, leaning into certain features
The idea is to get people thinking about what could happen when tools like these are released in the real world

And then they use that qualitative data to inform future designs and ethical frameworks.  Working together, Nowaczyk-Basińska and Hollanek came up with a series of made-up prototypes for deadbot apps, designed to reveal some of the thorny issues raised by this technology.  For the first scenario, they invented a character named Bianca, who finds an app called Manana, which “promises to resurrect your grandparents so that you can be a favorite grandchild forever,” Hollanek says. “So she uploads her grandma’s voice messages, texts

And she is able to then interact with a pretty good digital version of her grandmother, until her premium trial finishes — and the grandmother starts to advertise specific products to her.” Bianca “realizes that she maybe has done something wrong by uploading these private messages to a third-party server that now also uses her grandma’s image to sell specific products,” Hollanek says

This brings up issues related to the “dignity and postmortem privacy…of what we call the ‘data donors,’ whose data can be used to essentially power a deadbot,” he says.  This scenario suggests that “death with dignity” could soon entail honoring not only how people want to die, but also how they want to linger as simulations of their former selves — or if they want to linger at all

It might even mean adding new language to advance directives, spelling out people’s wishes for their digital remains.  The second scenario in the speculative design research is built around an imagined service called Paren’t, which proposes to preserve a parent’s AI-powered postmortem presence for their child

In this case, Hollanek describes a mother with a terminal illness who signs up “so that she can maintain a sort of active presence in [her son’s] future life,” Hollanek says. “She eventually dies, and the dad allows the boy to interact with his mom’s deadbot.” The ethics in this scenario are especially challenging because they involve children, who “have a particularly hard time understanding death, and so it can lead to a lot of confusion and potential distress,” Hollanek says

An examination of this sort of product reveals how particular groups, like minors, could be harmed by unfettered access to technology like this, he says.  And there are court cases that bear out that harm

In 2024, a 14-year-old boy’s chatbot-girlfriend begged him to, “Please come home to me as soon as possible, my love.” And he responded, “What if I told you I could come home right now?” He then killed himself.  Nowaczyk-Basińska can imagine a version of this scenario involving the AI mom in the Paren’t prototype
And then there’s the third scenario, involving an app named Stay, which raises a more subtle concern

As Hollanek explains: “An older man who knows he is getting close to dying decides to create a digital clone of himself for his adult children to be deployed after he passes away, paying upfront for a number of years.” One child is intrigued by the idea, but the other one “is deeply distressed and a little disgusted,” he says. “And so this [becomes a] question of mutual consent, in other words, the fact that both parties need to be happy with how the relationship might continue in this very bizarre and specific way.”  When a digital ghost goes away Across all three scenarios, a fundamental question that researchers are grappling with is how people will detach from postmortem avatars — whether users initiate that separation, or if it’s imposed upon them by, for example, a company going out of business

Hollanek tells me that this is already being studied as a sort of “second loss.” How long should we try to ensure digital replicas hang around: five years, 10, 50? And how should the living process the relationship when they continue to evolve, but their deceased interlocutor does not?  To explore these kinds of questions, Nowaczyk-Basińska and Hollanek supplemented the research dinners they held for ordinary people with a second set of focus groups
These were designed to tap insights from experts in technology and grief.  Some findings from the study are specific to each place they visited
Like tensions in Poland between technology and the role of the Catholic Church

Or in China, where researchers spoke with Daoist philosophers who were enthusiastic about the promise of a kind of immortality, and then Buddhist philosophers, who were concerned that we ought to be letting go
The researchers are calling for regulations and safeguards at the policy level

And new professionals who can support ethical use of AI in grief — like maybe in clinical settings, to carefully facilitate a final good-bye when one didn’t happen in real life.  Some of their fellow investigators go so far as to argue that deadbots should only be available with psychological supervision, to ensure that best practices are in place, and to minimize the risk of harm
There’s even a looming question of what will happen to AI agents that people have empowered to act on their behalf, as their humans start to die

Across all of the research sites in the digital immortality study, one thing, Hollanek says, that “people in different countries really aligned on [is] the idea that there is something deeply problematic about this particular type of technology being developed by a commercial entity alone without any explicit duty of care towards its customers.”  And of course, the implications of digital immortality research extend beyond personal loss

Like, what does it look like to animate historical figures? You can imagine the nightmare of political rulers who “live forever.” But there’s also the potential to keep the stories alive from survivors of conflicts, who would otherwise die and take with them lessons future generations could learn from

title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau
excerpt: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns Controversial vaccine researchers who have been pra
body: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m

body: Result is a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin the process of independence, delivering a decisive victory for supporters of Canadian unity and deepening divisions within the separatist movement
With nearly 1.9m votes counted, roughly 76% people supported remaining in Canada, while 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta

title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
excerpt: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms Mo
body: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday
Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese
But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”
Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”
The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status
